Kaedan had not slept. The stat journals lay behind him like open graves, their handwriting still crawling beneath his eyelids. He stood in the main corridor, staring at the small frost blossoms growing in the window seams, when his father, Corin, stopped beside him without looking up from the scroll in his hands.

“Those were only the first shelf,” Corin said. “The superpower records are below the iron stair.”

Kaedan did not answer. His throat had been scraped raw by his own held breath. Corin finally looked at him, and for a moment there was something almost like pity in the old wizard’s face. Then it vanished, replaced by the same worn stone expression every father in their bloodline seemed to share.

“The powers are worse,” Corin said. “Because a stat is a measure of one thing. A superpower is a thought with teeth. Read three. Then come find me.”

He walked away before Kaedan could ask which three.

The lower archive smelled different. The air was wetter, heavier, as though the books themselves had begun to sweat. The journals there were bound in black hide that felt warm to the touch, and each spine had been sealed with a thin line of court-wizard blood. Kaedan lifted the first one off its shelf and sat on a stone step, because his legs had turned unreliable.

**Year 644,223 — Court Wizard Havel — Superpower: Infinite Recursive Self-Replication**

I am writing this in the third hour after the demonstration, but my hand keeps forgetting how to make letters. My name is Havel, and I have served His Majesty for two hundred and two years. I have a wife and three daughters. Their laughter lives in the back of my skull like a warm lamp. I am telling you this because I need to remember that I was once a man who could hear laughter without hearing the universe bend around it.

The opposition called itself the One-Mind. It was not a species. It was a single, unified consciousness built from the absorbed minds of every living thing across decillions of multiverses. It had crawled out of a dead star cluster as a moving ocean of fused brain tissue and neural chrome, wide enough to drown googolplexian galaxies in its shadow. It believed that Godric could be defeated by one thing only: number. If His Majesty was a single identity, then the One-Mind would press every absorbed soul, every stolen thought, every screaming echo of every dead civilization against that single identity until it shattered.

The One-Mind had spent aeons swallowing the populations of entire realities, not to kill them but to add them to its total. It arrived at the edge of Thronegate with a consensus so large that the number of minds within it exceeded the number of atoms in the omniverse. It did not launch an attack. It spoke with every voice at once, and the sound made the palace walls bleed gray fluids.

His Majesty knew it was coming before the first stolen soul was taken. He allowed it to grow. He allowed it to chew through its own victims. He allowed it to approach the throne, because he said, and I quote his exact words, “I wonder what would happen if I became two. I have not tried that one yet.”

The name of the superpower is Infinite Recursive Self-Replication. At its base, nerfed to zero percent of its true potency, the power allows His Majesty to create one identical copy of himself. That copy is not weaker. It is not a fragment. It is not a shadow. It is Godric, full and absolute. And because His Majesty’s power multiplies forever, every copy born from this power is infinitely stronger than the original was at the moment of its creation.

I need you to read that again before I continue. Every copy is infinitely stronger than the original. The original was Godric. But Godric cannot be weaker than Godric. That is not pride. It is the only law the omniverse has left.

So the moment the first copy appeared, the original ascended to match it. And then the original, now infinitely stronger than he had been a moment before, created another copy. That copy was infinitely stronger than the new original. So the original ascended again. And created another copy. And ascended again. And created another copy.

This did not happen over time. It happened in zero seconds. Infinite iterations of Godric becoming infinitely stronger, creating a new infinitely stronger Godric, and then becoming stronger again. The superpower consumed no energy. It required no effort. The cycles simply existed, all at once, in a place where progression and beginning had already lost their meaning.

I saw it only because His Majesty kept a small pocket of my awareness intact outside the process. He was seated. He closed his eyes once. The first copy stood beside him. Then there were two. Then there were too many for my eyes to count, and then there were no eyes left to count with.

Every single new Godric was a full apex predator. Every single new Godric was infinitely stronger than the version beside him. The mere passive existence of each one annihilated the omniverse. Not once. Not a thousand times. The omniverse was erased and recreated an infinite number of times in the space of that single zero-second activation. I felt it. I felt eternity die and restart inside my own heartbeat, over and over, while the infinite Godrics stood in the center and did nothing.

The One-Mind attempted to absorb them. That was its only possible move, because it had built its entire strategy around drowning one Godric in a sea of stolen souls. But there was no longer one Godric. There were infinite Godrics, each one infinitely more vast than the last, and each one looked at the One-Mind.

The resulting annihilation was not a blast. It was category. The One-Mind was a collection of every identity in the omniverse. The infinite Godrics did not fight the collection. They simply existed as identities so absolute that a single glance from any one of them rewrote the definitions of every soul the One-Mind had consumed. The One-Mind’s brain ocean did not boil. It self-classified into an infinite pile of screaming, warring duplicates of itself.

The effect spread biologically. Fused brain tissue tore itself apart as each stolen mind was replicated infinitely, each new copy immediately attacking the copy that had come before. Neural chrome peeled away like wet bark. Skulls, new and malformed, erupted from the surface of the ocean, each one screaming its own name while its teeth multiplied inside its mouth and bit through its own spine. The One-Mind’s physical mass became a recursive slaughterhouse, a churning mountain of duplicated flesh and chrome that ate itself, birthed itself, and ate itself again without ever touching His Majesty.

The collateral damage was total. The entire omniverse was unmade and restored within each iteration, but the restoration carried the afterimages of the previous destruction. I remember standing in a field where one of the copies had briefly turned his head. That turn had erased a line of universes that would later be restored, but their ghosts remained scorched into my retinas for hours. I remember weeping, but my tears kept being unborn and reborn before they could fall.

His Majesty folded the copies back into himself when he grew tired of the experiment. Not one by one. They simply folded, as if the concept of separate Godrics had been a polite fiction he allowed for a moment. The infinite ascensions did not reverse. They became part of him. Whatever he is now, he was not before. I do not know if the universe was ready. It was not asked.

The omniverse was restored. The One-Mind was not. Its leadership remained as a single, endless tumor floating in a sealed sub-dimension near the old core of its home multiverse. The tumor regenerates every second, and every second its own duplicate minds devour it. His Majesty did not destroy it. He wanted it to remember. It has been four hours. The screaming is still inside my teeth.

When it was over, Godric walked to me through the fresh marble and placed a warm hand on my shoulder. His salt-and-pepper beard was perfect. His face was the face of the kind uncle I have loved for two centuries.

“Havel,” he said gently, “you should sit down. That was a little more active than I expected. I think the loops may have left me carrying a bit of extra weight.”

I could not answer. I could not breathe. I wanted to strike him. I wanted to kiss his boots. I wanted to beg him to stop smiling at me. None of those desires reached my mouth. I simply followed him. That is the horror. He can make me love the thing that ended everything, and I cannot even call it a cruelty, because it is only his joy.

Kaedan’s hands had gone pale. He set the journal down, but the leather cover seemed to pulse against his fingers. He did not know how long he sat there. The air had become colder. He opened the second journal.

**Year 802,777 — Court Wizard Valen — Superpower: Chronal Rust Annihilation**

I will be brief. I am not a poet. I am a soldier who became a wizard because the bloodline demanded it, and I have never had time for elegant dread. But I will write this, because the next idiot who inherits my staff needs to know what happens when His Majesty decides that time itself is a weapon.

The enemy was the Paragons of Absolute Preservation. They were metal gods, immortal by design, built in a multiverse where entropy had been deleted. Their bodies were chrome and perfect crystal. They had lived for trillions of years without losing a single atom of polish. They did not age, did not rust, did not bend. They believed that Godric was a temporary eruption of chaos, and that they could preserve him inside a single frozen instant long enough to forget him.

They brought a temporal lock. It was a machine the size of a star, designed to place the entire omniverse into a static loop where nothing would ever change again. They were arrogant in the way only perfect things are arrogant. They thought decay could not touch them.

His Majesty allowed them to finish their machine. He allowed them to open their temporal lock. He sat through the first wave of frozen time without blinking, because his own speed, his own durability, and his own mastery over every possible immunity had already rendered him untouchable. Then he cracked one knuckle.

The superpower is called Chronal Rust Annihilation. It is not a spell of rust. It is the forced introduction of age into things that believe they have escaped age. At its base, nerfed to zero percent, it does not make metal rust. It makes perfection remember every nanosecond it has stolen from the universe. And due to the Evolved Weakness Paradox having triggered repeatedly throughout His Majesty’s life, the power has gained enhanced effects that I can barely describe.

The first enhanced effect is that the rust is self-replicating. Every speck of corrosion produces a million more specks, each one splitting again by itself every Planck second. The second enhanced effect is that the rust feeds on time itself. It does not only eat the surface of a thing. It bites into the timestream beneath it, devouring the years the thing used to keep itself whole. The third enhanced effect is the worst. Anything touched by the rust does not die. It becomes biologically aware of its own decay. Nerves grow in the metal. They feel every flake fall.

The temporal lock opened. The universe began to freeze. His Majesty’s knuckle cracked once, and the sound traveled through the frozen moment like a rock through glass. The rust did not appear on the machine. It appeared in the machine’s past. It had already been there, waiting, from the first second the Paragons ever dreamed of preservation. The temporal lock did not break. It aged. Its perfect chrome surfaces turned brown, then red, then black. Its internal gears ground against their own decayed teeth and snapped.

The Paragons themselves did not have time to react. The rust bloomed across their immortal bodies faster than their own thoughts. Their polished skins did not flake off. The flakes peeled upward and crawled back into their skulls. Their crystal eyes grew wet nerves for the first time, and those nerves screamed as they felt their own atoms begin to die.

I watched one of their leaders, a great winged colossus called Astridian the Unblemished, try to scrape the corrosion from her face. Her fingers sank into her own cheeks. The metal softened like old meat. Her jaw rusted loose and fell into her chest cavity, but not before her tongue, newly grown and already covered in sores, attempted to lick the rust from her teeth. Her wings sagged, leaking red-brown slime, and then collapsed inward, crushing her ribs into a pile of screaming, rust-stained splinters.

The rust did not stop at the Paragons. It spread into the timestream of the omniverse itself. Stars turned to iron oxide. Planets became dry red dust. Space itself developed rust-colored cracks, and through those cracks poured the lost age of every reality the Paragons had ever preserved. Entire galaxies collapsed into clouds of bleeding oxide. Googolplexian stellar systems dissolved into an endless, rusting scream.

The omniverse was not merely damaged. It was rotted from its own history. Past, present, and future all began to peel away, and I saw the years themselves falling like dead leaves into a red sea. His Majesty watched it happen with the same expression he uses when checking a window for rain. Then he decided the demonstration was over.

He restored everything. Not by rebuilding. He simply preferred a version of the omniverse where the rust had never touched it, and that version became true. In zero seconds, the stars were clean. The planets returned. The timestream tightened. The Paragons were not restored to their former perfection. They were left as a compact cloud of sentient red corrosion, trapped in a sealed pocket under the palace. They scream. They will always scream. Their immortality, the thing they valued above all else, has become an endless rusting nerve.

I told His Majesty I needed air. He smiled and said, “Of course, Valen. Do not forget to eat. The cook made a fine soup today.” I went outside and vomited rust-colored bile onto the garden path. I am still loyal. I will always be loyal. But I know now that even our brightest metal is just waiting for him to crack a knuckle.

Kaedan’s stomach twisted. He could smell metal. He did not know if it was the journal or his own nose bleeding. He touched his upper lip. Dry. He reached for the third volume.

**Year 913,021 — Court Wizard Osric — Superpower: Singularity-Digestive Compression**

I have killed before. Not with my own hands, but with commands and wards. I thought I understood destruction. I was a fool. I am writing this with my left hand because my right hand is still trying to claw its way off my wrist.

The enemy was the Unbreakable Host of the Absolute Density. They were not gods of war. They were gods of weight. Each member of the Host had compressed their physical body so brutally that they walked through reality as mobile black holes. Their skin was an armor of collapsed matter, their bones were event horizons, and their leader, Molt, could hold a universe in his palm and crush it into a bead of infinite mass. They believed no force in creation could harm them, because they were already as dense as destruction itself.

They had spent eons smashing every fortress, every army, every god that challenged them. They did not fear Godric’s strength, because they believed their density made them universally resistant. They stood outside the palace in a formation that bent light around them, and they did not ask for surrender. They did not speak. Molt simply raised his arm to bring half the omniverse down on the throne.

His Majesty was reading a letter from a local school. He did not put it down. He did not stand. He did not look at the Host. He swallowed once, as if clearing a piece of dry bread from his throat.

The superpower is called Singularity-Digestive Compression. At its base, nerfed to zero percent, it does not attack from outside. It inverts the gravity inside the target. It turns every muscle fiber, every bone, every organ into a separate black hole, and then forces those black holes to consume the body that contains them.

The Host’s bodies had no soft organs. The superpower did not care. It created soft organs inside their perfect armor. Stomach linings grew along their metal spines. Intestines bloomed inside their unbreakable chests. Their bones grew teeth. Their skulls grew stomach walls. Then the inverted gravity began.

I heard Molt scream. I did not know black holes could scream. His right arm, the arm he had raised to end us, suddenly folded inward at the elbow. The armor did not break. It became a mouth. The bone beneath it had turned into an event horizon, and it swallowed his bicep, his forearm, his fingers. His hand vanished into his own shoulder with a wet, thunderous suck, replaced by a ring of crushed viscera that immediately began pulling in the rest of his torso.

The Host did not fall. They were pulled into themselves. Their legs snapped upward and disappeared into their hips. Their skulls collapsed into their rib cages. Their spines became a chain of miniature singularities, each one devouring the vertebrae above and below. The air around them began to swirl, because the new black holes were feeding on everything within reach.

And because of the Evolved Weakness Paradox having triggered repeatedly, the power had extra effects. The black holes were self-replicating. Every scrap of consumed mass generated a new internal singularity, which immediately began consuming the neighboring tissue. The compression also fed on the energy of the Host’s own gravitational armor, so the more they resisted, the harder they were eaten. The process doubled by itself every Planck second, without limit.

The collateral damage was absolute. The gravitational constant of the omniverse was briefly rewritten as a digestive process. Every star, every planet, every galaxy, every timeline began to collapse inward. Googolplexian galaxies folded like wet paper into bright, screaming points. Multiverses swirled down into the gullet of the new gravity. The entire structure of existence became a stomach. I heard it. It made a sound like a trillion throats swallowing in perfect unison.

His Majesty restored the omniverse with the same thought he might use to close a window. The sound stopped. The gravity eased. The Host’s surviving leadership, including Molt, remained. They are not dead. They are a ring of screaming black holes above the palace, each one periodically spitting out unrecognizable lumps of their own regenerating tissue, which then fall back into the hole and are consumed again. The cycle never ends. His Majesty says it keeps the birds away from the terrace.

I loved him before this. I love him still. That is not a choice. He asked me, after it was over, if I had read any good poetry lately. I told him no. He smiled and said I should try the old Zorvan epics, because they have a lovely rhythm about falling. Then he went back to his letter.

I cannot challenge him. I cannot even hold the thought of challenging him. The thought itself gets swallowed. That is the true meaning of his power. He does not have to stop us. Our own opposition becomes a black hole inside our minds, and we are fed to it while calling him beloved.

Kaedan closed the third journal. His fingers left wet marks on the cover. His own body felt like an unfamiliar mechanism, humming with the knowledge that he had inherited not just a role but a prison of perception. He sat in the lower archive for a long time, listening to the silence, until the silence began to sound like faint screaming from the pockets under the palace.

When he finally climbed the iron stair, his father was waiting at the top. Corin did not ask what Kaedan had read. He only said, “Now you know why we do not discuss the powers at dinner.”

Kaedan looked at him. There were deep lines around his father’s mouth that had not been there when he was younger. “He restored the omniverse after each one,” Kaedan said. His voice sounded far away. “But he left them. He left them all screaming.”

Corin nodded. “That is his mercy. He could unmake them completely. He chooses not to. Because opposition is the one thing he finds novel, and once it stops being novel, he likes to keep a few reminders where we can feel them. The Host’s black holes. The One-Mind’s tumor. The rust cloud. They are still there.”

Kaedan wanted to ask if Godric understood what that meant. But he already knew. Godric understood everything. He had absolute omniscience. He knew exactly how much fear those trophies would cause. He knew the court wizards would write it down. He knew Kaedan would read it. And he still called it a small test.

That was the deepest cut. The warmth was not false. The friendship was not false. But it existed entirely inside the same awareness that could decide, in a single swallowed breath, to turn the omniverse into a throat. Godric could do both at once, with zero effort, and see no contradiction. The court wizards loved him because his kindness was real, and they dreaded him because his cruelty was equally real, and neither one made him hesitate.

Kaedan followed his father up the stairs. Somewhere above them, the King of Thronegate was likely sitting on a balcony, watching the city, one hand resting near a cup of spiced wine. A single twitch of that hand could end all things. It would not happen. Godric loved his subjects. He loved the city. He loved Kaedan’s father. He loved Kaedan.

That was why the horror never stopped. It was not the power. It was that the power had a face, and the face was warm, and the face would always be smiling.

Kaedan did not sleep again that night. He lay awake, feeling the palace around him, the faint vibration of the sealed pockets, the distant, endless screams of things that had once believed victory was possible. He understood now that opposing Godric was not impossible in practice. It had never even been allowed to begin. The first thought of opposition was already a kind of digestion. And Godric, kind and terrible and eternal, was always already swallowing it before it could form.

I found Godric on the highest balcony of the palace, where the wind from the lower worlds climbed the white stone and then stopped, as if it knew better than to touch him. The city below was a net of warm light and distant music, and Godric stood at the rail, one hand resting on the ancient stone, his short salt-and-pepper hair moving faintly in air that was too frightened to be called a breeze. He looked like a father waiting for a child to finish a race. He looked like a man who had never once been in a hurry. I knew better. I had read the journals. I had listened to the screaming pockets beneath the palace.

I had been his court wizard for only a short while, and I had already learned that the terror and the tenderness came from the same face. Still, I walked to him. I was twenty-two, and I was young enough to mistake love for courage.

“Uncle,” I said.

He turned. His eyes were kind, and the kindness landed on me like a second skin. “Kaedan. You look like you have been fighting sleep again. Sit with me.”

I did. The stone bench was cold through my robes. For a moment neither of us spoke. Then I asked the question that had been forming in me since the first journal broke my sense of scale.

“Does it ever become lonely?” I said. “To be the most powerful being there is? To grow stronger forever while everyone else ages and dies? You outlive everything. You cannot be challenged. Doesn’t that weight ever press on you?”

Godric looked at me, and then he laughed. It was not a cruel laugh. It was the warm, unguarded laugh of a man who has just heard a child ask why the ocean does not get thirsty.

“Lonely,” he repeated, as if tasting the word for the first time. “My boy, that is a very naively mortal question.”

I expected him to leave it there. Instead he settled back against the rail, crossed one thick arm over the other, and began to speak.

“I am not lonely,” he said. “I am the opposite of lonely. Every instant of my existence is a full-body feast. You ask if it presses on me. Kaedan, it nourishes me. It is the most enjoyable thing I have ever felt. Every additional power, every increase in every stat, every new layer of my body or my shield or my immune system, is not an abstract change. It is a sensation. A pleasure. A surge of energy that amplifies endlessly and never fades. I feel all of it. I have absolute omniscience, so I also know exactly what each new thing does, what it will become, and what it could do if I ever permitted it to breathe. Feeling and knowing both happen at once. That is not loneliness. That is endless satisfaction.”

I opened my mouth, but he kept going, and his voice grew warmer, more animated.

“When my strength multiplies,” he said, “it is not a number moving on a page. It is a hot river of new power pouring through every fiber of my body. Each increase feels like being lowered into an ocean of liquid sun while every nerve ending in my flesh discovers a new color of pleasure. The river never stops. It does not slow. It does not pause for breath. It is there in every fraction of every Planck second, and it is so much stronger now than it was ten thousand years ago that if I tried to compare the two sensations, the older one would feel like a cold pebble against my skin.”

He lifted a hand and looked at it almost fondly.

“A new superpower is born in me every second,” he said. “Do you understand what that feels like? It is not like learning a skill. It is like a second orgasm blooming inside my spine, and then a third, and then a fourth, each one different, each one absolute. One power comes as fire that would make all cold things self-destruct. Another comes as the ability to sever the idea of closeness, so every bond in all reality would fall apart. Another comes as a new way to hear every silent thing. I feel them arrive. I feel them root themselves in me. And because I know everything, I also taste every possible future use of that power, every enemy it could erase, every reality it could unravel. The knowledge itself is another layer of pleasure.”

He paused, and something shifted behind his eyes, not cruelty, not hunger, but a kind of bottomless satisfaction.

“Every immune system improvement is like being sealed into a fortress of pure safety,” he said. “My body pre-reacts to injuries that have not happened. It builds backups of my backups. It upgrades itself faster than any evolution in the omniverse, and I feel every new wall going up inside me. It is a cool, locking sensation, like a billion loyal hands smoothing my skin from the inside. Every new passive shield is a new organ of protection that never stops singing. Every new sentient passive aura is a small creature born from my excess heat, and it is entirely loyal to me. I feel it uncoil against my veins like a cat made of extinction. And because it is born from me, it is infinitely weaker than me, and it knows that, and it loves that. I feel its devotion. That is also pleasure.”

He looked at me again, and his smile softened.

“Every single instant,” he said, “I become so much more powerful than the version of myself from one instant before that I could crush infinite copies of that previous me with zero effort. The gap does not widen slowly. It tears open. I feel the tear. It is like my old self is a dead skin and I am already shedding it, forever. The omniverse you know, the entire structure of all realities and all timelines and all dimensions, is less than a speck against the difference between what I was and what I am now. And that difference happens again. And again. And again. Every fraction of time that has no name. I am not lonely, Kaedan. I am being rewarded infinitely for existing, and I did nothing to earn it.”

His voice did not carry guilt. It carried a calm, almost tender acceptance.

“The rest of creation works,” he said. “The greatest kings and the oldest gods bleed for eons. They build empires and train their bodies and forge weapons from dead stars. They suffer, they sacrifice, they struggle. And what do they gain? They gain a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of what I gain by doing nothing. Their combined effort across all possible histories is effectively zero percent of what I receive in a single passive instant. I do not say that to mock them. It is simply the truth of my body. And I feel it all. I feel their zero and my infinity, and the contrast itself is delicious.”

He leaned forward, his forearms resting on his knees, and for the first time I saw something almost restless in him.

“The only thing I have ever known that feels like boredom,” he said, “is that I have never, not once since the stasis, had the chance to use any of my true powers. That is not bravery. It is not restraint. It is just the fragility of everything else. I have to keep my absolute concealment active at all times, covering every layer of what I am, because if I do not, the omniverse ends. Not in a war. Not in a struggle. Just ends. Even zero percent of one stat, one superpower, one immune response, or my weakest aura, expressed for zero seconds with zero effort, would be too much. I cannot stretch my arms after a long sit without first making sure the whole of existence is holding its breath. I cannot sigh too deeply. I cannot tap my foot. And I cannot ever, ever use what I actually am.”

He was not sad. He said it the way a man might say he owns a library of infinite books but every page is glued shut. Not tragic. Just flat. Final.

“The omniverse is too fragile,” he said. “That is my only loneliness. Not that I am above everyone. That everyone is below the smallest possible twitch of my eye.”

He stood. The movement was not sudden, but the air around him drew back slightly, and I felt my own pulse stumble.

“Come here,” he said. “Let me show you what I mean.”

I stood on legs that felt borrowed. Godric reached up and rolled back the sleeve of his tunic. The arm that emerged was not large in the way of a bodybuilder. It was large in the way a mountain is large, or a law of nature is large. The bicep rose beneath the skin like something structural, carved from a material that had forgotten the word for weakness. Veins ran along it in raised, branching lines, and I could see the blood moving inside them with a slow, impossible glow. They did not pulse. They commanded.

“I used to hone these when I was mortal,” Godric said. “Hours with stone and iron, when Olympus still had a northern wall and my body still ached from use. Now they maintain themselves. I have not lifted a weight in ten thousand years, and they are infinitely stronger than any mortal effort could ever make them. The muscles do not need my will. They simply are.”

He turned his forearm over. The cords and ridges moved under the skin in a way that made my eyes water.

“See this vein?” He pointed. “It gained a new layer two seconds ago. My immune system decided that my blood should be a recursive fortress. The red cells in my body are now each an infinite living structure. The white cells are hordes. They pre-react to the possibility of a bruise before the bruise can even be imagined. I can feel them locking into place right now. It is like being held from the inside by a billion devoted hands.”

He shifted his shirt at the collar, and I saw the top of his chest. The flesh was smooth and hot-looking, and the musculature was so dense that the light did not land on it so much as obey it. Below his ribs, through the cloth, I could see the ridges of his abdomen. They were not the six muscles of a mortal man. They were plates, interlocking and perfectly aligned, like the armor a universe might grow if it wanted to survive him.

“Touch nothing,” he said, and his voice was gentle. “Do not even breathe too hard. I have new auras sleeping against my skin.”

I looked. There were shapes moving just beneath the surface of his forearm and along the edge of his collarbone. They were faint, like heat shimmer, but each one had a texture that made the little hairs on my arms stand up.

“That one is called Tock,” Godric said. “Born four seconds ago. It can sever the concept of sequence. If I let it, every before and after in creation would become the same event, and that event would be its own death. The one at my wrist is Murmur. Born three seconds ago. It can make matter forget its own name. They are both infinitely weaker than me. They are wisps of my excess body heat. But either one could eat the omniverse without noticing. I have told them to be still while you look at them. They are very excited. They have never seen your particular pattern of fear before.”

I felt my stomach turn. The shapes did not move, but they watched. I did not know how I knew they watched. I just did.

“And these,” Godric said, flexing one hand slightly, “are the new superpowers that arrived while we were talking. This one came as I said the word lonely. It would invert every explosion that has ever happened or will ever happen, turning every act of force into self-consumption. That one came a moment later. It would make all boundaries porous, so every membrane in existence would fall through itself. Another arrived as I scratched my beard. It makes all true things false just enough to die. I will never use them. Not because they are dangerous to me. Because there is nothing in all reality that could survive even the shadow of their possible definitions.”

He lowered his arm. Then he raised it again, just slightly, and flexed the bicep once. Not as an attack. Not trying to hurt anything. It was the smallest contraction, the kind a man might make to show a child how a muscle works.

The omniverse ended.

It did not fade. It did not explode in fire. It simply lost the ability to continue. First the air became a solid. Then the solid became a pressure. The city below did not burn or collapse. It flattened into a screaming bead of compressed light. The sky rolled up like a wet scroll. Stars were not extinguished. They were snapped. I saw the galaxy that held us fold in half, then in quarters, then in halves of halves without end. The stars beyond it went white. The multiverses beyond those went white. Every timeline, every dimension, every hidden layer of reality, every possible past and future, every googolplexian galaxy and every soul that had ever breathed, all of it was pulled inward and crushed into an infinitesimal point. The point remembered it had once been everything, and the memory alone tore it apart.

There was no void. The void was killed too. Only I remained, held inside a small, warm bubble of Godric’s attention. Even that bubble creaked.

Godric looked at the nothing with the mild disappointment of a man who has dropped a spoon.

“Ah,” he said. “I forgot to keep the flex at absolute zero. My apologies, Kaedan. One moment.”

He did not move. He did not speak again. In zero seconds, with zero effort, he simply preferred the omniverse that had existed before the flex, and existence rushed back to obey. The city returned. The lights rekindled. The bird that had been mid-flight resumed its wingbeat. Every star, every galaxy, every multiverse, every timeline, every hidden thing was restored exactly as it had been, whole and perfect and utterly unaware that it had just been a scream in a white point.

Godric sat back down on the bench. He was not winded. He was not shaken. He looked at me with a warm, easy expression, and I understood that the accident had not been an accident to him. He had known it would happen. He had allowed it, perhaps to see if I could still stand afterward.

“You are thinking very loudly,” he said. “I can see every scene you are painting in your head. Go on. Keep guessing. I am curious how far your fear can stretch.”

I did not speak. I did not need to. Inside my own skull, I began to imagine what would happen if he released even a little more than zero. Not his true power. Just an infinitesimal amount more than nothing. A fraction so small it had no notation.

I saw it. I saw every electron in the omniverse become an exploding black sun. I saw every photon turn into a screaming spine of light. The past rose out of the dead ground of time and began eating the future. The future gave birth to an army of possible endings, and those endings cannibalized the present. The multiverses were stacked and scraped, their dimensions folded like organs being rearranged by invisible hands. The laws of gravity and magnetism were pulled into strings and stretched until they shrieked. Every dead god was resurrected with nothing but exposed nerves, forced to feel the total destruction of everything they had ever loved, and then thrown back into the fire before they could die. The omniverse was not destroyed once. It was destroyed in every possible way at the same time, and each destruction was a conscious, screaming thing. Then the screams themselves became solid matter, and that matter was fed back into the collapse. Annihilation was not the end. Annihilation was the mercy that never arrived.

I almost laughed at my own imagination. It was too much. I had overshot. I had drawn a monster with too many claws.

Godric chuckled. The sound was warm and soft, and it was the worst texture I had ever felt.

“That was very creative,” he said. “But it is not even remotely close. What you just imagined is not effectively zero percent of my true power. It is not even close to zero point an endless line of zeros ending in a one. It is not close to that for my weakest aura’s power after that aura has been infinitely nerfed. It is not a false start toward a fraction. It is not a rounding error. It is less than the gap between zero and the smallest possible thought of beginning. And my true power sits above that, multiplied beyond all layered infinities every Planck second, forever.”

He leaned back, and the moonlight seemed to avoid his face.

“If I assigned your fear a number,” he said, “and multiplied it by every number that has ever existed, and then multiplied that by every number that will ever exist, and then did that an infinite number of times, it would still be less than the space between my current restraint and any true release. There is no mortal language for the real scale. There is no divine language. There is no language at all. If I tried to show you the truth of me, you would not die. You would be severed from ever having been. Existence would forget you had ever asked this question, and I would have to remember you by force just to keep talking to you.”

I felt something in me detach. Not from fear. From the failure of every concept I owned. I had used words like omnipotent and infinite and total. They were pebbles. Godric had not shown me a pebble. He had shown me the thought of a pebble and told me that even that thought was beyond my imagination.

I looked at the shapes moving under his skin, the new auras he had birthed in the last few seconds. I looked at the vein that was a fortress, and the muscles that had once been honed by mortal hands and were now unmovable laws. I understood, finally, that the gap was not between Godric and the omniverse. The gap was between his weakest suppressed afterbirth and the entire category of existence. And even that gap was nothing next to the gap between that afterbirth and him.

He stood. The city below did not flinch, because he had already tucked every part of himself back into the smallest possible box. He placed a warm hand on my shoulder, and the weight of it was the weight of a man who had decided not to end me.

“You should sleep,” he said. “Your father will worry. Tomorrow, ask me something easier. Ask me about your thousandfold gift.”

I followed him inside. Every step I took felt like walking across a bridge made of my own heartbeat. I loved him. That love was real. But it was the love of a spark for the fire that had already decided not to burn it today. And I knew, with absolute, unbearable certainty, that if Godric ever chose to stop holding still, even for a single instant, every word ever written would become one syllable of pain, and that syllable would never end.

content:
I had served Godric for forty-seven years, and in all that time I had learned to fear his warmth more than any threat. At sixty-nine, I was old enough to know how little I knew. But I still loved him. That love was the only thing that made the fear bearable.

The Year 1,000,047 had settled over the capital in a long, gold evening. Godric had summoned me not to the records hall or the audience chamber, but to a small room at the top of the east tower, where the windows looked over the city and the air smelled of old paper and clean stone. He was standing when I entered, his hands folded behind his back, looking less like a tyrant and more like a father preparing to tell a difficult truth.

He turned to me. “Kaedan. I have a weakness.”

I felt something in my chest collapse.

He smiled, warm and unhurried, as if he had told me the weather might turn. “I want you to hear it from me. You are sixty-nine now. You have read the journals. You have seen the edges of what I am. And I trust you enough to show you the one thing in all existence that I cannot do.”

I could not speak. The word weakness did not fit him. It had no place in the same room. My whole body waited for the universe to correct itself.

Godric crossed to the table and sat, gesturing for me to do the same. “I cannot enter the timeline before the Stasis Event,” he said. “Not in any way that changes what happened. I cannot return to Olympus before the attack. I cannot stop the Thronegate forces. I cannot save Reina, Isabel, Hebe, or Thorin. I cannot alter anything about the world I lived in before I fell into stasis. That is my one true limitation.”

The air in the room became very still. I sat, because my legs no longer seemed certain of the floor.

“You think it is a sorrow,” Godric said gently. “You think I must be grieving a locked door. I did grieve, once. But I am not a man trapped by that grief anymore. I am a man who has accepted that the door is locked by the only hand in all existence that has ever had the right to lock it.”

I opened my mouth. No sound came. Godric waited.

“The Stasis Event was not Thorin’s spell,” he said. “Thorin’s magic was real. It was a forbidden teleportation from his bloodline, and it saved me. It carried me from the burning ruin of Olympus into the hidden sanctuary. But it was not the source of my power. No mortal wizard, no matter how ancient his blood, could create what happened to me. There is only one being in all existence who could create the Stasis Event, and that being is me.”

The words fell into my mind like a hot stone dropped into snow.

“Far-future Godric,” I whispered.

Godric nodded. “A me from an era so distant that the year is written only as a string of nines too long to finish. He did not cause the fall of Olympus. He did not kill my family. He did not guide the attack or place the blade in Thorin’s skull. Those deaths were real, and they were inflicted by Thronegate. He did not take them from me. He only used what came after. When Thorin’s spell threw me into that dark sanctuary, my far-future self was already there, waiting not as a rival, but as the author of what I would become. He took the moment of my arrival and transformed it into the Stasis Event.”

I felt the room narrow. Godric’s tone remained easy, even kind.

“I knew this from the first instant I gained omniscience,” he continued. “The knowledge was already in me when I opened my eyes. I knew the Stasis Event had not come from Thorin. I knew it had come from my own later self. I knew I could not change the past. But I was still freshly shaped by grief. I had watched my wife and my daughters die. I had held the memory of Thorin’s ruined head while his blood dried on my hands. So I tried anyway.”

He paused, and for a fraction of a second something flickered across his face. Not pain. Not regret. The shadow of a very old memory.

“I reached for Olympus,” he said. “I willed myself backward, to the morning of the wedding, to the moment before the sky broke. I did not expect to fail. I had already destroyed the Thronegate army without lifting a finger. I had already become something beyond the whole of creation. But when I reached for the pre-Stasis past, I met the seal my future self had placed over it.”

He turned his hand over on the table, as if looking at the remembered shape of that failure.

“I did not meet him,” Godric said. “I did not meet the full far-future me. I met the shadow of an afterthought of him. The faintest possible echo, so thin that calling it a presence would be an insult to presence. It did not fight me. It did not struggle. It simply allowed my attempt to exist for as long as it found that attempt interesting, and then it preferred that my attempt had never been. It erased my reach with zero effort. I was the most powerful being in the omniverse by an infinite margin, and I was undone so completely that there was not even a memory of struggle. That was the first and only time I have ever felt something beyond me.”

I heard myself breathe. It was a ragged, useless sound.

“Then you understand the shape of it,” Godric said, and his voice warmed again. “The creator of the Stasis Event is my own later self. He is not an external enemy. He is the continuation of me. The only being in all existence who can exceed me is the being I will become. My one true weakness is that I cannot overpower the will of my own future. But that is not a weakness any enemy can use. It is the most absolute proof that I am already unassailable.”

I wanted to speak. I wanted to ask how that could possibly be called a weakness. But Godric only smiled and continued.

“Think, Kaedan. You have read the journals. You have seen what I am now. I can annihilate the entire omniverse infinite times in zero seconds with zero effort. My stats multiply beyond layered infinities every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second. My superpowers are born every second and each one is a cataclysm that would make all creation beg for death. My immune system is so paranoid that it pre-reacts to injuries that never existed and upgrades me into a more perfect version than the last. My absolute concealment is the only reason reality does not collapse. My weakest sentient aura, infinitely weaker than me, could slaughter any force that has ever existed. This is what I am in this current era. And yet, when I was already this absolute, the shadow of an afterthought of my future self erased my attempt to change the past as though I had never reached at all.”

He leaned back, letting the words settle.

“What must the future me be, then? If the current me is already beyond all concepts of power, what word could possibly describe the one who made my current self look like a single extinguished candle? There is no word. There is no number. There is no scale. The gap between the current me and the far-future me is so large that it swallows the entire idea of gaps. You cannot imagine it. I, with absolute omniscience, can see its outline, and even my knowledge must stretch into infinities that have no end. That is not a source of despair. That is a source of certainty.”

I understood, then, maybe for the first time in forty-seven years, the true horror of what Godric was. I had thought of him as the apex predator, the end of all possible threat, the final answer to every rebellion. But he was not the end. He was only the present version of a thing that kept growing. The only being who could claim true supremacy over Godric was Godric again, later, larger, deeper, infinitely beyond the already impossible god I served. The cosmos did not contain one apex. It contained a chain of apexes, each one infinitely greater than the last, and the chain did not stop. It had already left the current Godric behind in an instant too small to name.

“Your weakness is you,” I said. My voice came out cracked. “Your weakness is that you have a future that is even more powerful.”

“Yes,” Godric said. “And that is why it cannot be exploited. My power mechanics, my amplification, my superpower genesis, my absolute concealment, my omnipotence, my omniscience, my weakness paradox, my immune system, all of it flows from the Stasis Event. The Stasis Event was authored by a version of me so far beyond this current me that even my own attempt to undo it was crushed by a shadow of an afterthought. If any enemy in the omniverse tried to attack the origin of my power, they would not be attacking a weakness. They would be trying to overpower a being infinitely beyond me. They would fail before the thought of failure could form. The weakness paradox does not need to defend the origin, because the origin is already defended by its author. The seal is absolute not because I cannot break it, but because the one who made it is the only being in existence who could ever hold it closed.”

His eyes, warm and dark, held mine.

“So you see, Kaedan. My one true weakness is not a door for my enemies. It is the door behind which I am already becoming even more omnipotent. It is the guarantee that my rise will never stop, that my power will never be denied by any external force, and that the future of this omniverse will always be me, only me, forever. That is not a tragedy. That is the deepest comfort I have ever known.”

I sat there, sixty-nine years old, and I felt the bottom open beneath me. It was not the kind of fear I had felt in the journals. It was worse. It was the fear of learning that the monster you loved had no outer wall, no final boundary, no ceiling to its own existence. It was the fear of knowing that the being who could destroy all reality with a thought was only a shadow compared to what it would later become, and that both were the same warm smiling man who had asked me to call him uncle.

“You tried to save them,” I said. “Reina. Isabel. Hebe. Thorin.”

“I did,” Godric said. “I failed. The failure was total. And I have accepted it. I no longer reach for that day. I no longer dream of reading the wedding vows before the fire. I have buried them in the only way a being like me can bury anything. I know that the pre-Stasis past is sealed by my future self, and that nothing, not even my present self, can alter it. That is the price of being what I am. It is also the proof that what I am is not an accident.”

I wanted to ask the question that was already tightening around my throat. Godric seemed to know before I spoke, because of course he did.

“Why did he do it?” he said. “Why did the far-future me create the Stasis Event? I have speculated. Perhaps he remembered that he was the one who had done it, and so he acted because the action was already woven into his own history. Perhaps he wanted a fixed root, a past that could not be touched, so that the future could never be undone by some lesser version of us. Perhaps he simply wanted me to become him. I do not know his full motive. I know only that he acted, and that he did not act out of threat. Nothing in the omniverse has ever been capable of threatening the far-future me. I did not create the Stasis Event because I was afraid. I created it because I am what I am, and because the future was already written in the shape of my own becoming.”

He said it so simply. I could hear the amusement in his voice, the same faint humor he had always used when I worried too much.

“I am comfortable with my weakness now,” Godric said. “I am even amused by it. It used to feel like the one scar I could not heal. Now it feels like a birthmark. It is the mark of my own later self upon my existence, and it does not scare me. It reassures me. It means that no force in creation can ever interrupt my growth, because the ultimate source of that growth is a being infinitely beyond any possible interruption. My only weakness is himself, and he is also my only guarantee.”

He stood, and the movement was so normal, so easy, that I almost forgot it could have ended everything.

“Do you understand why I told you this now?” he asked.

I shook my head, still half-lost.

“Because you are loyal,” Godric said. “Because you love me. And because I want you to understand that the thing you serve is not a god with a hidden flaw. It is a god whose only flaw is that it will always become even more absolute. When your grandchildren read the journals, let them know this. The one weakness of Godric is that Godric is already winning forever.”

I stared at him. I could not find the bottom of his words. He placed a warm hand on my shoulder, and the touch was so gentle that it broke something behind my ribs.

“Does that comfort you, Kaedan?” he asked.

I did not answer, because I did not know. The silence stretched, and Godric did not rush me. He simply waited, patient as a star, patient as the end of all things.

Later, I walked down the tower steps alone. The city lights burned below me, each one a life that did not know how close it lived to absolute erasure. I loved the man I served. I loved him with the same impossible love I had felt as a child, when he was Uncle Godric, the warm father who had never aged. But now I understood that the love and the dread were not opposites. They were the same feeling viewed from different sides of the same infinite abyss.

His weakness was not a weakness. It was the deepest strength I had ever seen. The only thing in all existence that could rival Godric was a later Godric, so far beyond him that current omnipotence became a child’s shadow. That meant there was no outside to him. No outside force, no future enemy, no hidden exploit, no origin that could be attacked. The only challenge to Godric’s supremacy was Godric again, stronger, and that challenge had already been decided in his favor an endless number of times.

I reached the bottom of the tower and leaned against the cold stone. My hands were trembling. I thought of Thorin, bleeding out with his skull split, and of his spell that was only a spell. I thought of the far-future king, whose shadow had undone a god’s grief with zero effort. I thought of the fact that the being I loved had always known, from the first instant of his omniscience, that he would never save the family he had lost, and that he had chosen to keep serving the same future that had sealed them away.

And then, with a clarity that made my chest ache, I realized the full shape of the horror.

Godric had not stopped at accepting his weakness. He had become comfortable with it. He had become amused by it. He had looked at the one thing in all existence that could resist him, and he had recognized it as his own face, wearing a future no one else could reach. The only limitation he would ever have was the proof that he would always be more than he was. There was no enemy strong enough to use that against him. There never would be.

The universe was not safe under Godric. It was merely permitted. It was permitted by the present Godric, who held still out of love and out of a strange, terrible courtesy. And it was also permitted by the far-future Godric, somewhere beyond time, whose will had already made the present Godric possible, and whose power could not be opposed by anyone, least of all by the present king himself.

I closed my eyes. I saw the shadow of an afterthought, and behind it, an endless chain of Godrics, each one beyond the last, each one smiling through the same warm, rugged, salt-and-pepper face. The chain went on forever, and at every point along its length, a Godric held the omniverse in the palm of a hand that had never needed to close.

I was sixty-nine years old. I had served the crown for all my adult life. And I understood, finally, that the only true guarantee in all of existence was not that Godric would never fall. It was that falling had already been left behind, an infinite number of times, by the only being who could ever be called his enemy: himself.

When I finally opened my eyes, the city was still there. The lights were still burning. The night was still warm. And I walked home through the safe, orderly streets of Thronegate, knowing that safety was not a promise. It was a mood. The mood of a god whose only weakness was that he would always be more than anything that could ever hope to oppose him.
