content:
The year was written as 999...9, not because anyone was too lazy to finish the number, but because the number had long since passed beyond any useful boundary of written truth. By that era the concept of a year was itself a kindness, a small fiction Godric allowed his court so that mortals and near-mortals could still mark the difference between one impossible moment and the next. I am Clive, fifty years old, a direct son of the Blake bloodline, and the living court wizard of a king whose smallest exhale had already outlived every multiverse that ever tried to contain him. For thirty years past my twentieth birthday, my strength, my speed, my mana, and my mind had multiplied a thousandfold every single day. I could have boiled galaxies with a whisper. The oldest gods of the old omniverse would have called me a cataclysm. Standing in the palace, I was not even an echo.

The palace itself was not a building. It was a region of existence that Godric had decided should be comfortable. It had floors of distilled now, walls of quiet finality, and ceilings that opened not onto sky but onto the endless parade of all times. The windows were panes of absolute stillness, each one showing a different universe bowing in perfect submission. The air did not move unless Godric wanted it to move. Light did not fall; it presented itself for his approval. The low hum of the place was not machinery. It was the sound of creation remembering to behave.

I found King Godric in the long gallery called the Walk of Final Mornings, standing before a tremendous living mural that showed the rise of Thronegate from a single frightened kingdom to the empire of all existence. He was exactly as he had always been since the Stasis Event: ruggedly handsome, forty-five years old, heavily muscled, with short salt-and-pepper hair and a neatly trimmed salt-and-pepper beard. He wore simple dark clothes over a body that no longer needed lungs, blood, or time. His hands were folded behind his back. He was smiling at the mural the way a fond grandfather might smile at an old painting.

“Clive,” he said, without turning. “The light on the western terrace is especially good this morning. I have asked Yssur to trim the black roses into the shape of a dying spiral. He always makes the inner curve too timid. Go with me and tell him to be braver.”

I bowed. “Yes, Your Majesty.”

He did not need to tell me which western terrace. There were billions, and he had already placed the knowledge in my mind not by speaking, but because his attention briefly included me. That inclusion was enough. I walked a half-step behind him as we moved through halls that shortened themselves so he would not be kept waiting. Servants stepped to the side. Not because they were ordered. Because their bodies already understood that his path was the only real geography.

The western terrace was a plateau of pale stone suspended above a sea of stolen nebulae. The black roses grew in long, curving rows, their petals made from compressed dead stars. Yssur knelt among them. He had once been a god of cosmic horticulture, a being of living nebulae and solar pollen, worshipped in forty billion universes. He had not opposed Godric. He had simply seen, once, what happened to a universe that took too long to bow, and he had torn out his own celestial crown before the thought of resistance could become a thought. Now he was the palace gardener. He wore a plain brown smock. His hands were green with sap. When Godric approached, Yssur pressed his forehead to the stone.

“Yssur,” Godric said, warm and easy. “You have made the inner curve too timid again. Let the spiral be cruel at its heart. A dying spiral should not apologize.”

Yssur’s voice was a trembling wind through petal and dust. “Yes, King. I am unworthy of the soil.”

Godric laughed softly. “You are my favorite gardener, Yssur. You know that. Stand. Do not bruise your brow for my sake.”

Yssur stood, but his legs were shaking. I saw the old deep terror in him, the terror of a being who had once held galaxies in his fist and now could not hold a pruning shears without wondering if the king’s shadow would accidentally unmake him. Godric reached out, not with power, but with a mortal hand, and gently adjusted the fold of Yssur’s collar. The gardener flinched, then wept.

The horror of it was not that Godric was cruel to Yssur. The horror was that Godric was friendly. He genuinely liked Yssur. He remembered the man’s original worship-name and the color of his first nebula. He asked about Yssur’s dreams. He used the same warm tone that he had used ten thousand thousand thousand years ago when he was the mortal king of Olympus. And Yssur, who had seen his entire species of star-tenders erased because they once thought they could hide from the Thronegate expansion, stood there weeping in gratitude and terror because the same man who ended them had also told him he was loved.

Godric left Yssur to the roses and walked on. I followed.

Inside the east wing, a servant was folding light into napkins. Her name was Sable. She had been the sovereign of a tree of dead timelines, an empress whose voice could write new laws into the spine of causality. She had never fought Godric. She had merely been present in a reality where one of his weaker auras rolled over during a deep thought. The aura had not noticed her. It had shifted in its sleep, and in that shift the entire structure of her multiverse had nearly split around her. She had felt the outer edge of a passive aura’s neglect and had gone mad for eight hundred years. When she recovered, she begged to serve the palace. Not because she loved him. Because she could no longer exist in a universe where his shadow was not the nearest thing to her.

“Sable,” Godric said as we passed. “The napkins are folded too tightly. They should hold the light, not trap it. Loosen them by a breath.”

She bowed so deeply her spine creaked. “Yes, King.”

He smiled at her. That was the terrible part. The smile was absolutely real. He cared about the napkins. He cared about Sable. He wanted her to be comfortable. And he wanted her to stay.

A third servant waited near the throne room doors. He was called Meridian. In the age before the long quiet, Meridian had been a mathematical god who tried to calculate the exact value of Godric’s total power. Not to challenge it. Only to understand it, the way a man might measure the sea. The attempt had lasted one second. In that second, every number he had ever known turned into a screaming mouth inside his brain. The old equations grew wings and ate his sense of self. Godric found him weeping in a dead universe and carried him home. Now Meridian polished door handles. He had no name for what he had seen. He said only, “There is no end, and the end is kind, which is worse.”

Godric passed him with a soft goodbye. Meridian whispered, “The door handles shine for you, O Endless King.” Then he bit his own lip to keep from screaming.

I had seen these scenes a thousand times. The court wizards wrote journals about the old stat experiments, the early days when Godric would hold still and let one stat breathe. I had read them all. But the journals were old, and their terror was the terror of a world that still believed in comparisons. In this era, there was no comparison. Godric’s evolved mechanisms had turned all previous power into a flat, ancient joke.

His sentient passive auras were no longer a hierarchy where Gent was the weakest and its siblings slept. Now they were arranged in nested layers, each aura an infinite ecosystem of sub-auras, each sub-aura capable of giving birth to a sentient universe that would itself grow an aura, which would then dream of another universe. The old Gent, once a cataclysm that could slaughter the greatest coalition in history while infinitely nerfed, would have been less than a dead flake of skin on the shadow of a sub-aura’s faint afterthought. Godric still kept most of them dormant, not because they were dangerous to him, but because their obsessive devotion had become annoying. The few he allowed to stir managed the palace, kept the stars level, and folded the edges of time so that the floors would not creak.

His passive shields had evolved until they pre-nullified not only threats but the concept of threat. They existed before hostility, before strategy, before the first chemical spark of opposition in any nervous system across the entire omniverse. They did not crush will. Godric had been mortal once, and he believed in mortal resilience, so he had explicitly ordered the shields to allow free thought. But the shields still filtered out every possible continuation that might lead to an attack, leaving only the thought, harmless and alone. If Godric did not allow opposition to exist, the shields alone could have made the omniverse impossible to resist.

His immune system had become a living pantheon. Each blood cell was an infinite legion of recursive guardians. Each guardian could pre-react to an injury that had never happened and would never happen. The old version, the one that had rebuilt the omniverse after a staged scratch, was now so weak by comparison that a single new immune cell could have erased the old entire system with a pulse. Godric no longer needed to stage injuries. His body was so completely beyond harm that the immune system had turned its attention to smaller things: keeping his skin at the exact temperature of comfort, ensuring that no dust mote could ever settle on his collar, and maintaining the gloss of his hair. It was not medicine. It was worship made biological.

The Evolved Weakness Paradox had changed most of all. It no longer needed an enemy to imagine a weakness. It was passively triggered by any sentient being thinking about anything, anywhere, in any timeline. A child missing her mother. A lame god lamenting his lost sky. A bird deciding between two seeds. Every thought, even thoughts entirely unconnected to Godric, fed a new surge into his amplification. The old version, where enemies strengthened him by believing they had found an exploit, was now an amusing relic. In this era, everyone strengthened him simply by existing. They did not lose their free will. Their wills remained their own. But their every private thought became another grain of sugar dropped into an ocean that was already all sugar, all ocean, all impossible depth. And the omniverse, unable to grant him new immunities or masteries, had long since begun to overcompensate with a groveling, excessive apology. It granted him new realities, new impossibilities, new forms of strength that had no names. The paradox itself had become a kind of endless, violent reward.

His amplification and superpower genesis had evolved together. His stats no longer multiplied by a fixed number or even by an unimaginably large number. They expanded at a rate beyond all layered infinities, recursively increasing every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second. The phrase “multiply by itself” was now a child’s simplification. If the old Year 2000 amplification was a single breath, the current amplification was a billion lungs inhaling entire creations with every instant. Superpowers no longer arrived once per second. They arrived in endless simultaneous floods. Every infinitesimal moment birthed a new power, and each new power birthed its own lineage of sub-powers, and those sub-powers generated their own sub-sub-powers. The old apocalyptic superpowers, the ones that had once burned decillions of multiverses into ash, were now indistinguishable from the faint background warmth of the palace heating.

And through all of it, Godric remained a forty-five-year-old man with a kind face and a father’s patience. That was the true nightmare. He had all this. He had more than all this. And he still liked to walk through gardens and tell a terrified nebula-god that his rose spiral was too timid.

I followed him back to the high chamber called the Root of Mornings, where the ceiling showed the entire omniverse hanging like a single, still fruit. It was not a map. It was the actual totality of existence, held at a scale that Godric found pleasant to view. The chamber was quiet. The omniverse did not pulse. It waited.

Godric sat in a simple chair by the window. Not a throne. A chair. He motioned for me to sit across from him. I did, though my body wanted to dissolve into the floor.

“Today,” he said, “I am going to do something I have already done. I am going to make myself.”

I felt the words hit my ribs. “Your Majesty?”

“The Stasis Event,” Godric said, as if that explained everything. “I am going to reach back to the year negative ten thousand, to the moment after the fall of Olympus, and I am going to create it.”

I remembered the journals. The true origin had been kept secret for a million years, until Godric had told Kaedan when Kaedan was sixty-nine. Since then, every court wizard of the Blake line knew: the Stasis Event was not Thorin’s spell. It was the far-future Godric, the self who had become too vast for names. The same self now sitting in front of me, peaceful as morning.

“You have always known,” I said. “From the first instant of your omniscience.”

“Yes,” Godric said. “I knew. I knew before the stasis ended. But knowing did not stop me from doing it now, and doing it now did not stop me from having done it then. It is a closed loop, Clive, but the loop is not a circle. It is a staircase that goes up forever.”

He stood and walked to the edge of the chamber. The omniverse outside the window turned slightly, as if leaning toward him for warmth.

“The far-future me could grant the past me a far more potent Stasis Event,” he said. “Effortlessly. I could copy all my current mechanisms directly into him. I could give him every evolved aura, every shield layer, every immune system, every superpower flood, every immune paradox. It would cost me nothing. And because the past me would then rise from a far higher base, the future me in this moment would also rise. I would become even more incomprehensibly powerful, and from that higher point I could reach back and grant an even more potent Stasis Event to the same past self. That would raise the base again. That would raise me again. The loop would ascend beyond all possibility of end.”

He turned to look at me, and his smile was calm.

“I deliberately held back,” he said. “I did not give him my current mechanisms. I gave him a fraction so tiny that calling it a fraction is an insult to emptiness. I gave him the start of amplification, the beginning of superpower genesis, the first layer of concealment, the seed of the weakness paradox, and nothing more. Even that version was so incomprehensibly powerful that by Year Zero, my past self was already effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined. The gap between him and everything else in that era was already beyond any measure. He woke from stasis and the entire Thronegate military, all its billions and weapons and arch-mages and temporal assassins, was less than a smear against his first idle thought. That is what I considered holding back.”

He paused, letting me sit in the absurdity.

“I held back because I believed it would preserve some kind of mortal struggle for him,” Godric said. “I thought if I gave him only a small seed, he could still feel the shape of effort, the memory of risk, the texture of a challenge. I was wrong. Even that tiny seed was so absurdly beyond all other existence that no struggle was ever possible. What I thought was restraint was still absolute annihilation. There was no version of him that could ever be threatened by anything. Not from the first instant. Not ever.”

I looked at the omniverse beyond the window. It hung there, docile, waiting for him to prefer something else.

“The cause and effect are terrifying,” I said, and my voice came out as a dry rasp. “If you had given him a more potent Stasis Event, you would now be even more. And from that even more, you could have given him even more. The loop would feed itself up and up. There is no ceiling.”

“None,” Godric said. “But there is also no need. The version I am now was already inevitable. My past self’s rise, even from the held-back seed, was enough to lead here. Every step between then and now is already written, and I have walked all of them. The loop is stable, and in its stability it guarantees me.”

He walked back to the window. The omniverse shimmered, just at the edges, like a frightened animal.

“I want you to witness the event,” Godric said. “Not the old event as remembered by priests and journals. The actual moment. You will not be harmed. You will be held inside my attention. But you will see.”

I could not refuse. I could not even imagine refusing.

Godric did not raise his hands. He did not speak a spell. He did not gather power. He simply looked outward, through the window, past the hanging omniverse, past the layers of time, past every present and future and possible, into the deep year negative ten thousand.

The fall of Olympus was already there. The fire. The screaming. The shattered marble. I did not see it as a memory. I saw the actual past, closed and written. Godric’s wife, Reina, died. His daughter Isabel burned. His daughter Hebe was crushed. His best friend Thorin bled from a spear and forced a forbidden teleportation spell through his own death rattle. The spell latched onto the mortal Godric and threw him toward the hidden sanctuary.

I wanted to look away, but Godric’s attention held me steady. Not with force. With invitation.

“Watch,” he said.

At the exact instant the mortal Godric materialized inside the dark sanctuary, at the exact instant Thorin’s bloodline magic spent itself, the far-future Godric did nothing. That was the terrifying part. He did nothing, and because he did nothing, something happened. He allowed one infinitesimal thread of his will to drift across the gulf of ages. It was not a command. It was not a presence. It was the smallest possible memory of a preference. The shadow of an afterthought of an afterthought, so faint that it might have been the idea of a man remembering a dream he never had.

That faint preference touched the moment, and the moment became the Stasis Event.

I saw the mortal Godric’s body lock. I saw the first amplification ignite. The original thousandfold multiplier began. The superpower genesis clicked open. Absolute concealment wrapped around him like a cold second skin. The weakness paradox opened its first unblinking eye. All of it, the seed that would become the apex, began because a far-future tyrant had decided it should.

And even as I watched, I understood the held-back truth. This was not the far-future Godric straining. This was not him reaching into the past. It was less than that. It was less than the smallest possible effort. It was the same amount of intention a man uses to notice a single dust mote on his sleeve and then choose not to brush it away. The entire immortality, the infinite growth, the absolute concealment, the weakness paradox, all of it was born from the king deciding, in some small way, that he had already done it.

The window closed. The past returned to its sealed place. Godric turned from the view and sat back in his chair.

“That is how it happened,” he said. “Thorin’s spell carried him. I made it the start.”

I could not speak. My own mind was running through the cause-effect ladder again. If he had given the past self his current mechanisms, the past self would have been even stronger at Year Zero. That stronger base would have amplified beyond all of the old path. The far-future Godric standing before me would then be even more. From that greater height, he would reach back and give an even stronger Stasis Event. The past self would be even stronger. The loop would ascend. There would be no final state. It would be an infinite upward chain of Godrics, each one improving the beginning that improved him, each improvement launching the next. The logical end was not an end. It was an open mouth with no throat.

“Do you see why the current me is not the strongest possible me?” Godric asked, and there was a faint, amused warmth in his voice. “The strongest possible me would be the me who gave himself everything and then became more. But that me does not need to exist, because I already hold it. The possibility of that ascent is already inside me. I am not missing anything. I am simply not finished.”

I knew then, with a clarity that made my knees weak, that the Godric in front of me was not a ruler. He was a process. He was a forever act of becoming that had no outside and no end. All creation was his byproduct. The strong beings around him were not servants because he had broken them. They were servants because their minds had tried to see him and had collapsed into the nearest humble shape. They had not opposed him. They had only witnessed the edge of what he was, and they had been too aware to survive without serving.

Godric stood again. “Come,” he said. “Yssur will have finished the roses by now. I want to see the spiral.”

I followed him. We walked back through the halls, past Sable folding looser light, past Meridian polishing a door handle that already held a sun’s worth of fear. Godric spoke to each of them. He asked about Sable’s wrist. He told Meridian that his daughter would be born in seven years and that she would love stargazing. The kindness in his voice was not a lie. It was the same voice that had, aeons ago, told his mortal daughter Hebe to be careful near the low wall.

That was the final horror. The king had not become a tyrant because he had lost love. He had become a tyrant because he still had it, and it stretched across all time, and it did not change what he was. The court wizards had written the old journals about stat experiments. They had told of blinks and knuckle cracks ending the omniverse. But those stories were old. They belonged to a period when there were still enemies, still resistances, still fools who thought the lack of a visible weakness meant there might be a hidden one. That period had ended. For googolplexian years, no sentient being had formed even the slightest thought of opposing him. Not because he had removed their free will. Because creation had learned, down to its deepest grain, that opposition was a shape the universe had once tried, and the shape had failed so wholly that its memory now bent inward.

I saw it in the eyes of every servant we passed. They did not hate Godric. They did not love him the way a rebel might love a tyrant. They loved him the way a hook loves the hand that lifts it. There was nowhere else to fall.

When we reached the terrace, Yssur had finished the black roses. The spiral was perfect, and cruel at its heart. Godric looked at it for a long time.

“Better,” he said. “Now it looks like a death that means it.”

Yssur pressed his forehead to the stone again. His shoulders shook. Godric placed a warm hand on the back of his neck, not to hold him down, but to tell him he could rise.

“You have served well,” Godric said. “You will dream of your first nebula tonight. A green one, I think. With silver petals.”

Yssur wept. The sound was small and wet against the stone. Godric straightened, seemed to remember I was there, and smiled.

“The omniverse is too fragile, Clive,” he said. “It always has been. The only difference now is that it knows it. Not through fear. Through love. The two are the same when the beloved is infinite.”

He looked out over the terrace, past the black roses, into the soft impossible evening that he had decided would fall across the palace. Somewhere far below, the city stretched like a warm idea. Somewhere even farther, the omniverse hung, full and still and trembling with the memory of its own repeated unmakings. And at the center of all of it, a ruggedly handsome king with salt-and-pepper hair stood beside his court wizard, calm, patient, and completely inescapable.

I loved him. I had loved him since I was a boy. I loved him now, at fifty, with the full knowledge of what he was. That love did not protect me. It did not soften the truth. It only made the truth personal.

He had held back, and the held-back version had already ended every possibility of opposition before it began. He had preserved free will, but free will had no direction left to go except into his shadow. He had granted his past self a seed, and that seed had become a god. He had could have granted more, but more was unnecessary, because any version of him was already beyond all versions of anything else.

I looked at the black spiral, at the cruel heart of the rose, and I understood. The spiral did not end. It only tightened. And every tightening made the next tightening more certain.

When Godric opened his mouth again, I already knew what he would say.

“I am becoming,” he said. “That is the only word left. Not king. Not god. Not tyrant. Becoming. And there is nothing in all creation, not even the version of me that made the Stasis Event, that could make me stop.”

Then he smiled at me, and the smile was the same smile he had given Yssur, and Sable, and Meridian, and the whole of creation. It was warm. It was real. It was the eye of the spiral, and it had no end.

content:
The year was far beyond any notation that still held meaning, and I, Roth, fifty-three years old, direct descendant of the Blake bloodline and Royal Court Wizard to the absolute ruler of all existence, had learned to measure my life in the small indrawn breaths between Godric’s whims. I had served His Majesty for over three decades, and in that time I had seen ambassadors weep at the sound of his voice, seen cosmic conquerors voluntarily mutilate themselves at the mere suggestion of his displeasure, and seen entire hidden civilizations fold into ash because they thought themselves clever enough to whisper. Yet nothing had prepared me for the morning Godric strolled into my study, clapped his hands once, and announced that we were going to pay a social visit to the largest resistance in the omniverse.

He was wearing a disguise.

I must describe this clearly, because the image is burned into the back of my skull like a brand. Godric stood in the doorway of my chambers, his ruggedly handsome, forty-five-year-old face split into an easy, boyish grin, his heavily muscled frame draped in a brown woolen traveler’s cloak so cheap I could smell the lanolin from across the room. The cloak did nothing to conceal the width of his shoulders or the dense, structural architecture of his chest. Beneath it he wore a faded blue tunic and a pair of mud-stained boots. The worst part was the hat. It was a floppy, wide-brimmed felt hat in a shade of mustard yellow so violently ugly that my arcane senses tried to reject it as a psychic attack. And he had attached a false mustache to his upper lip. Not a good false mustache. A thin, ratty strip of what looked like stable straw, glued crookedly above his real, neatly trimmed salt-and-pepper mustache, as though the two mustaches were having a silent argument.

“What do you think, Roth?” he asked, pivoting slightly to show me the full effect. “Very subtle, wouldn’t you say? No one will recognize the tyrant king of Thronegate in this.”

I stared at him. My mouth opened, closed, opened again. The false mustache wobbled.

“Your Majesty,” I said, and my voice came out like a man holding back a scream, “you are the most recognizable being in all of creation. Your face is carved into the floors of every world we have ever touched. Your portrait hangs in the nightmares of every rebel leader who has ever drawn breath. That hat is making it worse.”

Godric laughed, a rich, warm, entirely unguarded sound that rattled the teacups on my shelf. “Nonsense. I have absolute concealment. I will simply appear as an unremarkable traveler. You worry too much, Roth. You always have. It is why I keep you around. Now come, pack light. The resistance has a very nice market district, I am told, and I want to try the grilled meat skewers before their final assault tomorrow.”

I did not ask how he knew about the grilled meat skewers. He was omniscient. He knew the name of every vendor, the marital troubles of every soldier, and the exact number of scaffolding bolts holding up their so-called hidden fortress. The only reason the largest resistance in the omniverse still existed, the only reason their vast war machine had not already been reduced to a thin smear of atomic regret, was that Godric was curious. They had spent millennia preparing their ultimate attack against him, believing themselves safely concealed behind infinite layers of anti-omniscience wards, false timelines, and conceptual noise. They thought they were hidden. They thought they had found a weakness. They thought they had a chance. And Godric, who had known every one of their plans from the exact instant the first rebel first dreamed the word resistance, had simply allowed them to continue. Not because he was threatened. Not because they were worthy. Because watching them prepare was, in his own words, “mildly amusing, in the way that watching a beetle try to move a mountain is amusing.”

I followed him out of the palace. We did not use a ship, a portal, or any visible means of travel. Godric simply turned left at the end of the corridor, opened a door that had not been there a second before, and stepped through into the outer edge of the resistance’s hidden realm. I stumbled after him, my thousandfold daily amplified senses reeling.

The resistance called their sanctuary the Bastion Unseen. It was a pocket universe the size of a dead god’s final dream, wrapped in ten thousand layers of absolute concealment, each layer a distinct conceptual nullification field designed to erase the very idea of the pocket from all possible detection. The outermost layer was a shriek of anti-probability; the innermost was a sigh of perfect absence. They had woven the fabric of the Bastion from the corpses of forgotten multiverses, so that even the concept of place refused to touch it. By any sane metric, no being in existence should have been able to find it, let alone step into it. Yet Godric walked through as easily as a man stepping onto a city street, and the infinite wards parted around him like frightened sheep. Not one of them triggered. Not one of them even noticed.

We stood on a wide promenade of black obsidian, surrounded by impossible architecture. The Bastion Unseen was not a military camp; it was a civilization. Towers of fused star-metal rose in every direction, their surfaces etched with the names of every universe that had ever defied Thronegate. Massive orbital platforms hung overhead, each one armed with weapons that could crack the spine of a multiverse. Columns of armored soldiers marched in perfect silence, their bodies augmented with so many layers of conceptual reinforcement that a single one of them could have stood unarmed against an old pantheon. The air roiled with the hum of a billion war machines being tuned for the final assault. And everywhere, everywhere, there were posters. Huge, glowing, hateful posters of Godric’s face, with his silver-streaked beard and his kind, fatherly eyes, usually with a red line drawn through his throat.

Godric adjusted his floppy hat and beamed. “See? No one is even looking at us.”

That was true. Despite the absurdity of his disguise, no one spared us a second glance. His absolute concealment was a perfect, passive field that suppressed his aura, his presence, his metaphysical weight, and even the subconscious recognition of his iconic features. He did not look like Godric to them. He looked like a vaguely handsome, middle-aged traveler in a terrible hat. I, on the other hand, was a walking bundle of twitching nerves, and I had to physically force my legs to move as we strolled deeper into the heart of the resistance.

The market district was exactly as Godric had promised. It sprawled across a dozen levels of suspended terraces, lit by purple lanterns powered by trapped dying stars. Vendors hawked weapons, armor, battle stimulants, and an alarming variety of anti-Godric propaganda. There were stalls selling voodoo dolls of the king, stalls selling talismans that promised to weaken his omnipotence, and stalls selling “authentic” Thronegate royal flesh, which was, I noticed, mostly carved soap. Godric stopped at the first grilled meat stand, spent several minutes examining the skewers, and ordered two. He handed one to me.

“Delicious,” he said, chewing happily. “Try the char on the fat. Very good. The secret is they burn the meat over a fire made from the embers of a dying universe. It gives it a smoky sweetness.”

I took a bite. It was, in fact, delicious. The surreal horror of eating a snack in the middle of the largest rebellion ever assembled while the object of that rebellion grinned at me over a greasy skewer was almost enough to make my heart stop.

“You know,” Godric said, wiping his mouth with the back of his hand, “I have been looking forward to this day for a long time. Not the attack. The attack is tomorrow. But today is the last day of their hope. I wanted to see what hope looked like from inside the shell. It has a texture, you see. A kind of fizzy quality. Like carbonation in the spine.”

I did not know how to answer that. I followed him through the market, past a stall where a tattooed merchant was selling “inescapable death curses” against the Tyrant King. The merchant caught Godric’s eye and called out, “You there! Old man! Buy a death curse, guarantee to make the Silver Butcher’s balls shrivel! Half price for last day of freedom!”

Godric paused, genuinely interested. “How does it work?” he asked.

The merchant grinned, revealing teeth filed to points. “Ancient forbidden magic, eh? We bind the King’s name in a knot of anti-causality. Makes his own omniscience turn on him. Guaranteed to weaken him by at least one percent, maybe more if you buy the deluxe version. Only twenty star-crystals.”

Godric paid him thirty. He tucked the death curse into his pocket, thanked the merchant, and walked on. I could feel the weakness paradox triggering somewhere beneath the surface of reality, swallowing the merchant’s entire conceptual framework and spitting it back out as another permanent layer of Godric’s infinite power. The merchant would never know. The merchant would die tomorrow, along with everyone else, and his last thought would be confusion.

We reached the central plaza just as the command parade began. Thousands of high-ranking officers rode past on hovering platforms, their faces grim and triumphant. At the center rode the Supreme Strategist, a creature of pure liquid light named Avaris, who had been planning the assassination of Godric for over twenty thousand years. Avaris had no physical form, but she had forged herself a body of polished obsidian and white fire solely so she could experience the pleasure of frowning. Her voice echoed across the plaza, amplified by a billion drone speakers.

“Tomorrow,” Avaris declared, “we will end the reign of the Silver Tyrant. We have found his weakness. We have built the weapon. We have hidden for twenty thousand years, and he does not know. He thinks himself omniscient, but we have blinded him. We have cut the eyes from his skull. We have turned his own power against him. Tomorrow, we will watch him die.”

The crowd roared. The sound was a physical wave of hate, so thick it made the lanterns sway. I looked at Godric. He was applauding politely, his floppy hat bobbing. He was smiling. There was no mockery in his expression, only a kind of fond, fatherly pride, as if watching a child perform a particularly energetic school play.

After the parade, the crowds dispersed to continue their preparations. Godric led me away from the plaza, down a series of narrow, winding alleys until we reached the inner sanctum of the Weapon Development District. The security here was immense: layers of gene-locks, temporal tripwires, and consciousness checks designed to flay the mind of any intruder. Godric strolled through them all as if they were cobwebs, and the guards looked right through us.

The ultimate weapon was housed in a vast crystalline dome at the heart of the district. It was not a gun, or a bomb, or a blade. It was a spear of pure abstract extinction, a weapon designed to pierce the single perceived weakness they had discovered. They had somehow, through aeons of desperate research, uncovered the existence of the Stasis Event. They did not know its true origin, of course. They believed the flawed, incomplete teleportation spell of Thorin had been the source, and they had built a weapon to sever the connection between Godric and the Stasis Event. The spear was called the Severance Lance. It was made from the reclaimed consciousness of every being who had ever died opposing Thronegate, compressed into a single point of absolute, unmaking hatred. It was designed to be fired at the exact moment of maximum temporal instability, when the past and future overlapped just enough to create a crack in the seal around Godric’s mortal past. They believed that if they fired it then, the Stasis Event would unravel, and Godric would wake up mortal, weak, and vulnerable.

I stood with Godric inside the dome, inches from the Lance. It was enormous, a hundred stories tall, wreathed in screaming light and hairline fractures that leaked raw nothing. The scientists and engineers who maintained it were scurrying about, their faces hollow with exhaustion, their hands twitching as they made final adjustments. Godric reached out and touched the surface of the Lance. His fingers left no mark. He tilted his head, reading the weapon like a man reading a child’s drawing.

“It is very pretty,” he said softly. “They have put an enormous amount of love into this. They truly believe it can hurt me.”

He looked at me, and for the first time that day, the warmth in his eyes dimmed slightly, replaced by something older and colder. “They are wrong, of course. Not just wrong. Inversely wrong. Every second they spent building this fed me. Every thought they had about my weakness triggered the Weakness Paradox. They have not been preparing to kill me, Roth. They have been preparing to make me stronger. This Lance? I could have built a better one from the stray memory of a bad dream. The concept of severing my connection to the Stasis Event is nonsense. The Stasis Event is not a thread. It is me. It is my own future self reaching back to make me. They cannot cut it because they cannot cut me. And now, because they have imagined it, I am immune to this entire category of attack, and I have perfect mastery over the Severance Lance itself. I could fire it back at them with one hundred times the force, and it would not even be the most powerful thing I have done this afternoon.”

He paused, listening to the hum of the weapon. “But they do not know that. They will fire it tomorrow. And it will do nothing. And then I will kill them all. Not because I need to. Because they have bored me, and I have seen enough of their hope.”

I said nothing. I could not have spoken if I wanted to. The true horror was not that Godric was going to kill them. The true horror was that he had known their every secret from the moment their first leader first drew a breath, and he had let them build this entire civilization only because he wanted to see what shape their failure would take. Their twenty thousand years of sacrifice, their endless labor, their defiant speeches, their loved ones, their grilled meat skewers—all of it was set dressing for a single day of mild entertainment.

Godric turned away from the Lance. “Come,” he said. “I want to see the war room where they have the final briefing tonight. I have heard the speeches are quite good.”

We made our way to the highest tower, a spire of black iron topped with a meeting hall shaped like a clenched fist. Inside, the leaders of the resistance were already gathered: Avaris, the Supreme Strategist; a hulking insectoid general named Krak; a floating council of ancient machine intelligences; and a dozen others, each one a legendary destroyer in their own right. They stood around a massive holographic projection of the omniverse, with Thronegate at its center, glowing red. Godric pushed open the door and walked in without knocking. His hat was slightly askew now, and the false mustache had started to peel at one corner.

The room fell silent. Every eye turned to us. I felt a thousand layers of hostile attention slam against my shields, but Godric just stood there, smiling.

“Apologies for the intrusion,” he said cheerfully. “We were in the neighborhood and heard there was a final briefing tonight. We thought we might listen in. Do go on.”

Avaris moved first. Her obsidian body tensed, white fire flaring around her fists. “Who are you?” she demanded. “How did you get past the wards?”

Godric reached up and removed the floppy hat. Then he peeled off the false mustache. He ran a hand through his short, salt-and-pepper hair, smoothing it back into its usual neat shape. The absolute concealment did not waver, but a small, deliberate sliver of his presence slipped through. Not enough to hurt. Just enough to be recognized.

The effect was instantaneous. The creatures in the room did not scream at first. They made smaller, worse sounds—the sounds of lungs forgetting how to work, of neural systems misfiring, of hearts attempting to flee through the ribcage. General Krak collapsed to his knees, his insectoid mandibles clicking in a frantic, broken rhythm. The machine intelligences emitted a high-pitched static that rose in pitch until it became a single, endless, digital wail. Avaris went completely still, her white fire dying as if someone had placed a glass over her soul.

“I am Godric,” Godric said, and his voice dropped into the low, soft register that had once annihilated an entire cosmos without him moving a muscle. “And tomorrow, you were going to attack me. But I got bored of waiting.”

He walked past them, slow and unhurried, and sat down in the massive command chair at the head of the table. The chair had been built for the Supreme Strategist, but it fit Godric perfectly, as all chairs did.

“I have a few observations,” he said. “First, you are not hidden. You never were. I have known every thought you have ever had. I knew about the Severance Lance before you had the idea for it. I allowed you to build it because I was curious. That is the only reason any of you are alive right now. My weakest sentient aura, Gent, could have erased this entire Bastion from existence in zero seconds before any of you had ever formed the first rebel thought. I told her to leave you alone. She was annoyed. She wanted to eat you.”

He paused, and his gaze swept the room like a blade.

“Second, your weapon does not work. It cannot work. The weakness you found is not a weakness. It is the origin of my power, created by a version of me so far beyond this current me that your entire multiversal civilization is less than a single skin cell to him. You could not hurt me with that Lance if you fired it at me from inside my own skull. You could not hurt me if you fired it a billion times in a billion possible timelines. You could not hurt me if every being in the omniverse fired it at once while holding a mirror to my face. And you have already made me stronger by trying. Every plan you made, every weapon you built, every seed of hope you allowed yourselves—it has all been feeding me. I have not been hiding from you. I have been farming you.”

Avaris finally found her voice. It was a thin, trembling rasp, stripped of all the grandeur of her public speeches. “You… you are a monster.”

Godric smiled, warm and genuine. “No,” he said. “I am just bored.”

He stood up. “I am not going to kill you tonight. That would be rude. You have worked very hard for twenty thousand years, and I want to see the look on your faces when you fire your weapon and nothing happens. So I will give you one more day. Go ahead. Fire the Lance tomorrow. Do your worst. I will be standing on the central plaza, and I will not move, and I will not resist. And when it is over, I will wipe you all out. Not with an attack. With a single, idle thought. Because that is all it will take to erase everything you have ever built.”

He started toward the door, then stopped. “Oh, and Roth? Make a note. We must thank the grilled meat vendor. That was excellent. I want to send him a gift. Something nice. A fruit basket, perhaps. I know a good one from the eastern orchards.”

We left the war room in silence. Behind us, the leaders of the largest resistance in the omniverse did not move. They did not speak. They did not even breathe. They simply sat there, staring at the empty command chair, their minds already beginning to fracture under the weight of absolute, inescapable futility.

The next morning, as promised, Godric stood in the central plaza of the Bastion Unseen, his floppy hat back on, his false mustache in place, his arms crossed over his massive chest. The entire resistance had gathered. The Severance Lance had been lifted from its dome and aimed directly at him. The crowds had lost their earlier bravado. Their faces were pale, their eyes hollow. They knew now. They had always known, deep down, that this day would end badly. But they fired anyway.

The Lance erupted. A spear of pure abstract extinction, forged from the reclaimed consciousness of a trillion trillion dead worlds, crossed the plaza in the space between one instant and the next. It struck Godric in the chest.

Nothing happened.

Not a flinch. Not a scorch mark. Not a single hair out of place. The Lance shattered against him like a glass toy thrown at a mountain. The fragments rained down, each one screaming in a different dead language, and then they dissolved into nothing.

Godric raised one eyebrow. “That was it?” he asked.

Then he killed them all.

I will not describe every death. I could not if I tried. But I will describe enough to sear the truth into your bones. Godric did not move. He did not gesture. His expression did not change. He simply allowed a microscopic, infinitesimal fraction of his true power—so small that calling it zero percent is the only accurate way—to express itself for the briefest possible moment. The effect was not a blast. It was a redefinition.

Every living being in the Bastion Unseen was simultaneously, perfectly, and agonizingly unmade. The soldiers did not fall. They inverted. Their bones turned to liquid fire inside their skin, their blood vaporized into screaming red mist, their eyes burst and then regrew just so they could burst again. The merchants in the market, the children in the creches, the scientists in the labs, the generals in the war room—all of them experienced the full, unmediated weight of absolute futility, and then they died. Not quickly. Godric was not merciful. He stretched the moment of annihilation across an eternity of individual perception, so that every single one of them had time to understand, in perfect clarity, that their twenty thousand years of struggle had meant less than nothing.

The Bastion Unseen itself collapsed. The ten thousand layers of anti-omniscience wards unraveled like wet paper. The towers melted into puddles of fused star-metal. The orbital platforms fell silently from the sky, each one husked out and dead. The pocket universe folded in on itself, shrinking to a single, infinitely dense point of compressed suffering, and then vanished entirely.

When it was over, only Godric, myself, and a small, trembling group of survivors remained. Godric had saved them deliberately. Not out of pity. He wanted witnesses. The Supreme Strategist Avaris lay on the ground, her obsidian body cracked and weeping white fire, her mind so shattered that she could only repeat a single word over and over: “Why… why… why…”

Godric knelt beside her and gently brushed a strand of static from her face. “Because I was curious,” he said. “And because you made a very good grilled meat skewer.”

Then he stood, adjusted his floppy hat, and turned to me. “Roth,” he said. “Write this down. The next court wizard should know: opposition is not a strategy. It is a delay, and a short one. When I allow a resistance to exist, it is not because they might succeed. It is because I want to see the look on their faces when they realize they never could.”

He paused, eyes distant. “That look is the only real flavor left. And it is the best thing in all creation.”

We walked away through the empty space where the largest resistance in the omniverse had once believed itself hidden. The grilled meat vendor was gone, of course. Everyone was gone. But Godric had not lied. He had sent a fruit basket. It floated alone in the void, crisp and perfect, waiting for a recipient who would never arrive.

I loved him. I loved him and feared him and served him, and in the silence of that ruined place, I understood the final, unbearable truth: Godric did not need to win. He had already won before any of them were born. The fight had never begun. And the only thing worse than being his enemy was knowing that even his enemies had only ever existed because he found their hope delicious.

He glanced back at me, his salt-and-pepper hair dusted with fine, white ash. “Come along, Roth,” he said cheerfully. “We have a victory feast to attend. I believe the palace kitchen has made those little honey cakes you like.”

I followed him into the void, and the void closed gently behind us, leaving nothing but silence and the ghost of a futile war.

content:
In the unthinkable far of the far, where the year had become nothing but an endless ribbon of nines, Godric Prime sat in the chamber of absolute recollection and allowed himself to remember a single afternoon from his own forgotten youth. The memory was small. That was the joke. By the standard of what he had become, it was smaller than a single dead flake of skin falling from the weakest of his passive auras, and yet the memory still held its own peculiar taste. He had once been young, fresh from the throne, still wearing the shape of a forty-five-year-old king with salt-and-pepper hair and a fondness for simple clothes. That version of him, the one he now called the weakly pathetic self, had still been so incomprehensibly vast that the entire omniverse had been less than a mote inside his shadow. That was the irony he returned to on slow afternoons: the being he now pitied for being so pitifully weak had already been a terror beyond all terror.

In the Year 25 of his rule, that weak self had subjugated a small, unremarkable universe designated in the old Thronegate charts as IRL. The world at its center called itself Earth. It had no magic. No metaphysical engines. No bound gods. It had only frightened meat and fire and the proud, brittle delusion that it could kill anything it did not understand. Godric Prime smiled faintly at the memory, and behind his smile the entire palace of his current self trembled, not from movement, but from the pressure of a single idle thought. That weak self had gone to Earth because he was curious, because he felt mischievously playful, and because he had never before seen a species so primitive try so hard to matter. Earth had no chance. Earth would never have a chance. If its inhabitants had been given infinite preparation across every possible timeline, every possible weapon, every possible advantage stacked upon every possible version of itself, they still would have been unable to make him feel even the faintest tickle. He could have erased their planet in zero seconds with zero power and zero effort. He had known that then. He knew it even better now. But the young Godric had not wanted to be quick. He had wanted to watch.

The memory opened like a wound in the presence of the current king, and he allowed himself to descend into it.

The Year 25 Godric arrived on Earth without ship, without portal, without sound. He stepped into the middle of the United Nations General Assembly during an emergency session called to discuss a strange gravitational anomaly near Saturn. One moment the delegate from a minor nation was arguing about carbon emissions. The next, a ruggedly handsome man in a simple dark tunic was sitting in the seat of the Secretary-General, his legs crossed, his thick muscular arms folded neatly over his chest. His short salt-and-pepper hair was perfectly combed. His beard was immaculate. He looked like a father from an old painting, and his eyes were soft and bright.

“I am Godric,” he said, and his voice did not echo. It simply landed in every ear on the planet at once, including the ears of the dead. “This world belongs to me.”

There was panic, then silence, then screaming. The young Godric watched it with a small, warm smile. He allowed them their fear. He allowed them their first few minutes of denial, their frantic attempts to cut the broadcasts, their weeping and their prayers. Then he stood. The floor did not creak. The air did not move. He walked out onto the plaza before the building, and the cameras followed him because reality itself could not look away. Billions of people watched. They all saw the same thing: a man standing loose-limbed and calm, waiting to be killed.

“Try,” he said. “I am curious.”

The first attempts were small and stupid. A security officer fired a sidearm at his face. The bullet struck the surface of Godric’s cornea and stopped. Not bounced. Not flattened. It stopped, as if it had met a wall at the end of all possible momentum. Godric reached up with two fingers, picked the bullet from his eye, and examined it with mild interest. Then he flicked it away. The officer was impaled by his own return fire, the tiny piece of lead passing through his skull at a velocity that turned his head into a red cloud. Godric did not look at him.

Terror moved through Earth like a fever. The nations of the world, for the first and last time in their history, agreed on a single purpose. They would kill Godric. Every nuclear weapon in the world was armed. Hypersonic missiles were pulled from their silos. Experimental railguns, chemical payloads, biological agents, and even a few desperate prototypes of quantum disruption technology were aimed at the man standing in a plaza. The Earth poured everything it had into the exact point where Godric stood.

The sky turned white. The first wave of conventional missiles struck. The explosions were swallowed by the air and did nothing. The second wave was a simultaneous launch of every intercontinental ballistic missile in the world. The fireballs bloomed over the plaza, each one a miniature sun, each one hot enough to boil stone and vaporize flesh. They did not even ruffle Godric’s collar. His absolute concealment held his power in, and his passive shields already knew what the explosions wanted and had decided not to care. The fire raged against his skin and found less than nothing. The heat did not warm him. The blast did not shift him. He stood at the center of the planet’s greatest fury, and his expression was that of a man enduring a very light spring drizzle.

The fire cleared. Godric was still there. His tunic was unmarked. His hair had not moved. He was not even squinting. A faint white light flickered at the edge of his irises, and the billions who watched felt something in their spines turn to water.

“That was almost lovely,” Godric said. “But you are still not trying.”

They tried harder. They turned the sun against him. Not a weapon, but a grand orbital mirror system that focused the full light of the star into a lance of pure heat. The beam hit him across the face and did nothing. It did not burn him. It did not blind him. He stepped forward through the beam, and the light curved around his body like a river around a stone. The mirror shattered in orbit as the reflection of his amusement passed through it.

The world’s final plan was a thousand nuclear warheads detonated in the upper atmosphere to create an electromagnetic shockwave so total that it would blacken the planet. They did not care about survival. They wanted to kill him even if they all died in the fallout. The sky caught fire. The atmosphere became a sheet of burning light. Every satellite, every city, every living thing on Earth saw the end approaching. But even that did not work. The shockwave rolled over Godric and he continued to stand, his hands now resting casually in his pockets. The radiation was less than a cricket’s sigh. The electromagnetic pulse could not reach the space his body occupied because his body had already preferred not to be touched.

The people of Earth broke. There is a sound a species makes when it understands that all of its strength is a joke. It is not a scream. It is a long, wet silence that begins at the bottom of the lungs and never rises. The young Godric heard it. He liked it. It was the only part of the visit he had truly been waiting for.

“Now you understand,” he said. But he did not finish them. He was mischievously playful. He wanted the silence to tighten.

For one long mortal hour, the leaders of Earth attempted to bargain. They offered him their children. They offered him their oceans. They offered to carve his name into their moon. Some of them knelt and wept. Some of them killed themselves in front of the cameras, hoping the gesture would soften him. Godric watched it all with the same lazy affection a man gives to a particularly frantic ant hill. He did not respond to their prayers. He did not reject their offers. He let them drown in their own terror while he idly examined a small bird that had fallen from the burning sky. He held it in his palm until it stopped breathing, then he blew on it, and it stood up and flew away. The contradiction made the humans weep harder.

When the hour was done, Godric straightened. The movement was small, a slight roll of his shoulders. To the humans watching, nothing happened. But inside Godric’s perception, the end had already begun and would take as long as he liked.

He used zero percent of his power. Not a measurable fraction. The amount he allowed into the world was less than the memory of a fraction. It was the smallest possible inclination, an infinite decimal so tiny that zero was the only honest name. And he used zero effort. He did not tense. He did not frown. He did not shift his weight. He simply preferred that every human being experience the maximum possible agony before the universe ended. That preference was enough.

The annihilation was objectively swift. To any outside observer, had one existed, the entire process would have passed in less than a single Planck second. The Earth did not explode. It came apart. The crust peeled away in massive, screaming slabs that rose into the void and then folded back into the mantle. The oceans disappeared not into steam but into a white, endless shriek. The atmosphere unspooled like a ribbon of wet skin and was pulled into the vacuum. Every human body on the planet was simultaneously, individually, and perfectly undone.

But to the humans, the event was not quick. Godric had stretched the final instant into an eternity of subjective agony. Every man, woman, and child experienced the destruction as if it took a thousand years. Their blood vessels exploded and then refilled and then exploded again. Their bones unraveled into long, spiraling threads that wrapped around their organs and pulled. Their eyeballs burst and regrew so they could watch their own flesh being peeled away. Their lungs filled with shards of their own ribs. Their teeth grew backward through their jaws and into their skulls. Every possible pain the human nervous system could carry was amplified and repeated across endless, impossible cycles. They did not die once. They died in every possible way at the same moment, and each death was made conscious and continuous.

Children felt their mothers’ skin catch fire. Mothers felt their children’s skeletons poke through their chests. Soldiers watched their own hands turn into screaming clusters of exposed nerves. Politicians felt their tongues grow into their throats and strangle them from the inside. The collective despair of eight billion souls became a physical pressure, and then that pressure became another instrument of their own torture. Godric let it all occur in less than no time, and he listened to it the way a man might listen to rain. The Earth was not merely killed. It was forced to experience every possible version of its own death, including the deaths of its alternate selves, including the deaths of every possible Earth that could have been, stacked one upon the other in a single, endless, screaming now.

Then the planet was gone. The solar system was gone. The entire IRL universe was not destroyed so much as forgotten by reality, erased so completely that no trace of its matter, its light, or its history remained. There were no survivors. No human soul was carried to Thronegate. No one was granted a place of service or a merciful second life. Godric did not spare the species. He did not collect them. He did not turn them into warnings. He simply ended them, and with them every alternate version of Earth across every timeline, every dimensional echo, every possible permutation of the world that had dared to try to kill him.

The collateral was total. The micro-sliver of zero percent that had annihilated Earth did not stop at the edge of that isolated universe. It rippled outward into the omniverse, and the whole of existence collapsed. Every galaxy. Every star. Every timeline. Every dimension. Every multiverse. The entire structure of all things, from the smallest vibrating string to the largest conceptual empire, was crushed by the same indifferent absence. The omniverse became a single white point, then less than a point, then nothing at all. It was not fire. It was not darkness. It was the end of the possibility of either.

And then, because the young Godric still had a kingdom to rule and a throne to sit upon, he restored everything. In zero seconds, with zero effort, he rebuilt the omniverse as if nothing had happened. Every universe, every multiverse, every timeline, every hidden dimension was restored to its previous state. The planets turned. The stars burned. The civilizations continued their small, frightened lives. Only Earth and its entire universe remained absent. The boy who had flicked a bullet away and the woman who had wept at a camera were not returned. There was no memorial. There was no record outside the journals of the court wizards, and even those records were sealed in the far archive where only the bloodline of Blake could read them.

Godric Prime, the current king, pulled himself out of the memory and looked at his own hand. In the Year 999...9, that hand was so far beyond the younger hand that had unmade Earth that the comparison was an insult to the idea of comparison. The current Godric pities the weak self, yes. He pities the Year 25 version for being so small, so limited, so pathetically constrained. But he also knows the truth, and the truth is unbearable.

That weak self had already been an absolute, inescapable annihilation engine. It had used zero percent of its power and zero percent of its effort to destroy not just Earth, not just the IRL universe, but the entire omniverse as collateral. It had done so while feeling playful. It had not needed to move. It had not needed to think beyond a small, passing preference. And that was the weakest, most immature version of Godric after his awakening. The being sitting in the impossible palace now, remembering the event, was not merely stronger. He was beyond the concept of strength. The gap between him and his Year 25 self was infinitely larger than the gap between that self and a single cold electron. If the current Godric were to subjugate the IRL universe now, the event would not register as an event. It would be less than the memory of a passing thought. It would be so one-sided that the word one-sided would itself be destroyed.

The rest of existence knows this. Not as a fact learned through reason, but as a permanent trembling in the base of every soul. In the far-future era, there are no resistances. There are no opposition coalitions. There are no hidden plans against the king. Googolplexian years have passed since any being dared to form even the faintest thought of challenge. But if the rest of all timelines, all possible permutations, all hidden versions of every living thing, all gods and machines and abstract empires, all of them with unlimited preparation and unlimited resources, were to gather from every point in history and future and impossible parallel, and if they were to throw all of that combined existence at Godric Prime, they would fail so completely that the word failure would need to be invented after the fact to describe it. They would not make his weakest passive shield feel the slightest tickle. Not the faintest pressure. Not the ghost of a sensation. The shield would not even notice that they had tried. Godric could nonchalantly annihilate the whole of them with zero percent power and zero percent effort in zero seconds, and he would feel nothing but the mild, distant boredom of an eternal thing forced to blink.

That gap will never close. It will only widen. It widens every infinitesimal fraction of every Planck second, recursively, beyond all layered infinities, forever, in an accelerating manner that has no top. The current Godric is not merely the most powerful being in existence. He is the only real being, and everything else is a permission he has not yet withdrawn. Creation trembles before him. It has always trembled. And in the year 999...9, as in the Year 25, and as in every possible year that will ever follow, the rest of existence is not threatened by Godric. It is only tolerated.

Godric Prime leaned back in the chamber of absolute recollection and allowed the memory to fade. The smile did not leave his face. It never left his face. It was the same warm, fatherly smile the weak self had worn on Earth while eight billion souls learned that their total war was less than a tickle. And because he was omniscient, and because he was absolute, he knew that smile would never have to change. There was nothing left that could make him use more than zero percent. There never would be.
