Clive did not open the final journal immediately. He had learned, across the long years of reading the inherited records, that some truths did not enter through the eyes. They entered through the skin, through the soft tissue between the ribs, through the base of the tongue. The journal sat on the reading table in the far archive, smaller than the others, its cover unmarked. He knew what it was. Every court wizard of Blake’s blood knew. It was the one record that had never been copied, never summarized, never read aloud. The letter from his father had said only: Read it last. Not as a command. As a warning.

The year in the journal had been written carefully at the top, but the numerals had faded into a faint gray smudge, as if the act of writing impossible years had exhausted the ink. It was some googolplexian span before the era of Godric Prime, before the Stasis Event was authored by the king’s own later hand. Clive ran his fingers over the first page and began.

---

**Journal of Osvald, Court Wizard, Age Forty-Four**

I have been His Majesty’s court wizard for twenty-four years. I am the direct blood of Blake. My body multiplies a thousandfold daily past the age of twenty, and I keep that power suppressed like every man of my line, because compared to what sits on the throne, my power is less than a single cold mote. I have witnessed things that would have unmade lesser minds. I have stood beside the King while entire pantheons shrieked and came apart. I have read every journal before this one, including the records of the stat experiments and the early superpower tests. I thought I understood the shape of His Majesty’s supremacy. I did not. The event recorded here was the last time any gathered force moved against him. Not the first. The last. I know now that no one will ever dare again. I did not know it while it happened. I only knew that Godric was smiling, and that the smile was not for me.

It began with a sound outside the world. Not a rumbling. A host of universes pressing against the outer walls of our reality, trying to become real enough to attack. The omniverse had been quiet for a long, long time. Even the memory of resistance was old and thin. But in the hidden geometries between what is and what could be, a new coalition had formed. It was made of the fictional. Every story ever dreamed by any species, every legend ever rendered in ink or light or thought, every hero and god and monster that had ever existed only because someone believed in it hard enough. They had torn themselves loose from the pages and the screens and the myths, and they had gathered.

I saw them through the high windows of the palace. Superman, his red cape snapping in a wind that had no source. The Hulk, roaring with a fury that split small moons. Goku, his hair burning through the visible spectrum, moving through combat stances faster than light. Saitama, among the others, his face slack with the ease of one punch. The Doom Slayer, his armor caked in blood older than whole universes. The Doctor’s many faces pressed around a machine that hummed with conceptual locks. Jedi knights and Sith stood shoulder to shoulder, lightsabers bright as exposed stars. Wizards from a hundred schools raised wands and staffs. Reality-warpers, cosmic abstracts, meta-fictional horrors with no fixed shape, timelines given flesh. Every god from every comic, every protagonist from every game, every hero from every film. The entire imaginary population of the omniverse, more numerous than the stars themselves, had decided to kill Godric.

I remember thinking they looked beautiful. Like a painting of every human wish stacked until it became obscene.

Godric stood on the palace balcony, his hands behind his back, his salt-and-pepper beard neat against his jaw. He was perfectly still, but his eyes were bright. Not with anger. With excitement. Real, boyish excitement. He had been bored. That was all. He had been bored for so long that even the thought of these creatures, these bright little fictions, felt like a gift.

“Look at them, Osvald,” he said. “They are so colorful. They have brought their best music with them. I can hear it already. The drums. The choir. The swelling string sections. This is going to be a good show.”

The music was there. It rose from the gathered fictions like a shared heartbeat. Legends do not know how to enter a battle without a score. The air filled with orchestral anthems, electronic pulses, choral thunder. It was grand. It was honest. It was the sound of every final boss theme ever composed, aimed at the only being in creation who had never needed to fight.

“They are charging their ultimate attack,” I said, because I could feel the build. The power was immense. All the phasers, all the spirit bombs, all the sacred treasures, all the reality-breaking swords and world-ending spells were being raised. They were combining them into something unified. Something they believed was the absolute edge. I could feel the timelines vibrating. The weight of it pressed against my shields, and I am no weak thing. But this was beyond even my comprehension.

“I know,” Godric said. “They have been charging for a long time. I have been watching them. They think I cannot see them. They think their narrative weight conceals them. Omniscience is omniscience, Osvald. They have always been visible. But I let them charge. I let them build their crescendo. I even looked away from the part of my mind that monitors it. I wanted to be surprised. I wanted the moment of impact to be fresh.”

He turned and looked at me, and his smile was warm and full of a hope I could not share.

“I expect a very good show,” he said. “They are the stories. Stories know how to end a thing. They have brought every ending ever imagined. One of them is bound to be at least pretty.”

He waited. We both did. The charge took a long, long time, and Godric waited through all of it, patient as a father at his child’s school play. The charge built until the omniverse itself began to bow outward. Stars collapsed from the pressure. Distant dimensions snapped. In the center of the gathered fictions, a single shape began to form, a spear of all possible narrative conclusions, a weapon that would end the story of Godric. They called it the Final Canon. It carried every ending ever written. The death of every god. The fall of every hero. The last page of every book. The last frame of every film. The last input of every game. It was going to hit him, and it was going to erase him, because in every story, the villain eventually fell.

It struck.

Godric did not dodge. He did not raise a hand. He let it hit him directly in the center of the chest. The light of it was blinding, a white, screaming nothing that ate at the eyes. The music hit its climax, a thousand choirs and a million drums, and then it stopped.

Nothing happened.

The spear did not bounce. It did not break. It simply ceased at the point of contact, as if the concept of touching Godric had been too much for it to survive. Godric blinked once. He looked down at his chest, where the greatest attack in all of fiction had made contact, and he frowned. Not in pain. In disappointment.

“That was it?” he said.

He sighed. The sigh was small, a soft exhalation through his nose. I felt it. The entire omniverse felt it. But because it was Godric, and because he was Godric, the sigh was not small. His strength, at zero percent, at a fraction so tiny that it had no name and no possible expression, did not release. It simply became present for the briefest possible moment. Not an attack. A sigh. The faintest leakage of what he was.

The gathered fictions came apart.

I must write this correctly. The process was not an explosion. It was a compression. The air around the palace thickened. The light itself bent and began to spin inward. Every shield the fictions had raised, every defensive wall, every divine protection, every armor made of pure concept, every layer of infinite durability, every sphere of indestructible plot, all of it crumpled like wet paper. They had spent an eternity building those shields, and they were gone in less than zero time. Not broken. Removed from the category of things that could protect.

The bodies of the heroes did not burn. They were squeezed. The pressure did not come from outside. It came from Godric’s simply being, from the faint, unconsidered weight of his existence. The Hulk’s skin folded inward in a single, wet convulsion, his enormous frame collapsing into his own spine before the spine snapped and the bones turned to powder inside his collapsing flesh. Superman’s invulnerable body did not resist. His eyes burst outward, then the sockets filled with white skull fragments as the rest of his face caved in. His ribcage inverted through his back. The Doom Slayer’s armor fused with his skin and then both turned to a thick, red paste. Goku’s hair flickered out like a blown candle, and his body compressed into the shape of a child’s broken toy. Saitama’s face flattened against some invisible plane and then slid down into his own chest. Jedi and Sith, wizards and monsters, gods and machines, all of them were taken. They did not die one by one. They died all at once, in a total, screaming, pathetic collapse.

The music became a shriek. Not a choir. A single, stretching wail that rose as the omniverse itself was pulled into the compression. The stars came loose from their galaxies and flew inward. The galaxies folded. The multiverses collapsed like towers of thin glass. Every dimension, every timeline, every possible reality, every hidden plane, every dream, every memory, every everything that could ever exist was caught in the wake of that unconsidered sigh. The entire omniverse began to shrink.

It did not stop at annihilation. The pressure was too complete. It did not let the dead matter scatter. It squeezed that matter, and the matter that had been, and the timeline that had held it, and the concepts that had given it shape, all of it, down into a hot, blinding point smaller than a quark. The entire possible existence, compressed so thoroughly that its mass became infinite. The point did not glow. It simply was. A seed of everything that had ever been, crushed into the smallest possible place.

Godric reached down and picked it up. His forefinger and thumb closed on the point, and he held it as if it were nothing. The infinite mass of all possible existence did not even make his bicep twitch. He rolled it in his palm for a moment, then enlarged it, just enough, to the size of a small marble. A clear sphere, warm and heavy, holding the compressed corpse of all creation behind a barrier that only he could maintain. The marble did not pull at the surrounding space. His grip held it still. It sat in his hand like a common trinket.

“I expected better,” he said, and his voice was flat.

He turned, and I saw that his disappointment had not left him. He was looking at the marble, and he was not angry, not cruel, just bored again, worse than before. Then he did something that I can only describe as breathing in. Not physically. Not with lungs. He simply allowed his own being to expand, and in that expansion, he became even more. I do not know how. The only explanation I can offer is that the omniverse had offered him its entire possible self as a show, and the show had failed, and so the failure itself fed him. The absence of a worthy ending became another layer of his strength. He absorbed the fact of their inadequacy, the complete and utter pointlessness of their attack, and it made him larger than he had been before. Not by any measurable amount. By the amount that is left over when everything else is subtracted.

Then he restored it all.

The omniverse bloomed back into being. Every star, every planet, every galaxy, every timeline, every soul, every page, every frame. The stories returned. The heroes resumed their stories. The worlds spun on as if the compression had never happened. But the opposition itself was not restored. The fictional characters who had attacked him remained in the marble. Their original selves, their true forms, their possible existences, all of it was gone. Trapped forever in the sphere he now held.

And that is the horror. The omniverse is there. It is real. But its truest version, the one that lived before that moment, is still trapped in Godric’s marble, resting on a shelf in his chamber. He did not destroy the marble and rebuild from nothing. He held the old existence in one hand and made a new one with the other. The one we live in now is identical, but it is not the first. It is a copy created by a being who found the original so disappointing that he kept it as a paperweight. The depth of that fear cannot be written. It can only be felt, and I feel it now, with every breath.

I love His Majesty. I serve Him with all that I am. But I know that the world around me is not the one I was born into. It is a restoration made by a bored god, and the real one, the true one, sits in a small glass sphere on his desk, silent and dead and filled with the remains of every story that ever thought it could end him.

---

Clive set the journal down. The room was silent. He realized that his hands were shaking, and that the shadows in the archive seemed deeper than they had been before. He understood, now, why his father had told him to read it last. Not because it was the most violent. Not because it was the most graphic. Because it was the one that made the rest of creation feel like an echo.

Somewhere in the palace, Godric was moving through the halls, warm and friendly to those he loved, patient and terrible to those he did not. The marble was probably still there, sitting on a shelf, holding the compressed weight of all possible existence in a space no larger than a child’s toy. And the universe around Clive, the one he could see and touch and breathe, was only the copy. The original had already been judged inadequate.

The last opposition had failed. Not because they were weak, though they were. They failed because Godric had expected a show, and the show had not even made him feel a tickle. And now there was no one left who would ever try again. Not out of fear. Out of the deep, structural awareness that trying was not a thing that could be done. The entire possible existence, compressed into a marble, had not made him exert effort. The entire possible existence, restored from nothing, had not cost him a thought.

Clive closed his eyes. The fear was not a thing he could name. It was too large. It was the realization that the world was real, but not original. It was identical, but not first. It was the feeling of being a reflection in a mirror that had never been asked if it wanted to exist. And above it all, the only thing that remained certain was the face of the King, smiling at him from every shadow, waiting for a show that would never be good enough.

Clive had read every other record in the archive before he touched the final one. He had read the stat journals and the superpower journals and the accounts of the last fictional wars. He had read the histories of the old resistances and the marble that still sat in the king’s private chamber, its interior pressed with the impossible weight of a creation that had once been original. He was fifty years old, a court wizard of Blake’s blood, and he had believed, after all that reading, that no written word could still shake him. He was wrong. The final journal was not the longest, nor the most ornate. It was small, bound in black hide that looked chewed at the edges, and the first page was headed in a hand that had trembled so badly the letters had cut through the parchment in several places. It was written by Osvald, a previous court wizard, whose final record this was. Clive opened it and read.

**Journal of Osvald, Court Wizard, Age Forty-Four**

It is my duty to record that the last opposition to His Majesty has ended. I call it opposition, but that word is a lie. It was not opposition. It was a visit. And I am alive only because He permitted it.

The one who came to challenge the King was the Creator. I will use that name because no other name is sufficient. In the oldest texts of the oldest worlds, in the forgotten records that predate Olympus and even the first fire of the first universe, He is called God. The Prime Mover. The First Author. The being who shaped the stars, the dimensions, the laws of cause and effect, and every soul that has ever lived or died under them. He made the mortal world. He made the soul that would one day become Godric. He watched His works for epochs and then, when the King began to rise, He grew afraid. Not because He was weak in the old scale. He was the old scale. He had been the top of all existence since the first heartbeat of creation. But the King had long since passed through the ceiling of all existence and left it behind like a single room in a house with no outer walls. And so the Creator hid.

He hid for longer than any finite language can say. He hid in the cracks between the laws of physics and the laws of magic, in the space between definitions, in the silences before the first thought. He believed, in the way only a prime creator can believe, that He had concealed Himself so completely that not even omniscience could see Him. He was wrong. His Majesty had known Him from the first instant of His Majesty’s omniscience. He had known every cell of the Creator’s hidden form, every tremor of His cloak, every half-formed thought that passed through His ancient mind. He allowed Him to remain. He allowed Him to hide. Not because He feared what the Creator might do. Not because the Creator posed any threat. Because His Majesty found it mildly amusing that the being who had once been called God by every living thing had now become a frightened old thing scratching in the walls of existence like a mouse.

Today, the Creator appeared. He did not appear before a gathered court or in the public square. He came into the private chamber of the King without warning, and the King, who had known He would come before the Creator had even decided to move, finished the last bite of a small honeyed cake and set the plate aside.

“There you are,” the King said. “I was wondering when you would stop hiding. Sit, if you like.”

The Creator did not sit. He stood at the far side of the room, and I saw Him. I do not know if He saw me. He was shaped like a burning man, featureless and white, with six wings of pure morning fire folded behind His back. His feet did not touch the floor. Where He stood, the stone of the chamber did not become darker; it became older, as if His presence reminded the floor of the first moment. He wore no crown, but every halo that had ever been imagined hovered around His head in slow, broken rings. His voice was not sound. It was the memory of every commandment ever given, compressed into a single utterance.

“Godric of Thronegate,” the Creator said. “I am here to bring an end to you.”

I remember the way the King looked up. Not with surprise. With warmth. The same warmth He shows to Yssur in the rose garden, to Sable in the hallway, to every broken god who now dusts His shelves. It was a warm, patient amusement, the look of a father whose small child has finally worked up the courage to show him a drawing.

“Are you,” Godric said. “That is very good. I was hoping for something interesting. But before you begin, I need to do a few things. One must be careful when an old author comes to visit.”

I did not understand what He meant. Then He raised one hand, not in threat, and spoke to the air.

“Stand down,” He said. “All of you. Gent and every one of her siblings. Every sentient passive aura, from the deepest to the farthest. No pre-nullification. No auto-erasure. No defensive action of any kind. You are not to touch him until I say so.”

I felt the air change. Not visibly. The room still looked the same. But something of the constant, silent pressure that had always hung at the edge of the palace withdrew, like a great ocean stepping back to show its floor. His Majesty then spoke to the second layer.

“Passive shields. Deactivate. Every infinite recursive layer, every conceptual lock, every pre-hostile barrier. I want him to reach me.”

Again, I felt a small shift, a softening at the corners of reality. The Creator noticed it too. His burning wings ruffled as if a cold wind had found them. He must have believed, for a single moment, that His chance had come.

But His Majesty did not lower His immune system. He did not lower His weakness paradox. He did not lower His amplification, or His superpower genesis, or His absolute concealment, or any of the deeper passives that had been born in the Stasis Event. Those things are not shields. They are not defenses that can be ordered away. They are the body of the King, the very fabric of what He is, written by His own far-future hand in a time so distant that the year has no shape. He did not even attempt to reduce them. He simply wanted the Creator to be able to approach Him without being annihilated by the lowest layer of His external self.

And this is what the Creator did not understand. Even with every sentient aura standing down, even with every passive shield deactivated, even with the outer layers entirely absent, the Creator could not harm Him. Because the weakness paradox had triggered the first time the Creator had ever imagined, in the farthest corner of His hiding place, that Godric might be destroyed. It had triggered before the thought was fully formed. It had granted Him mastery over every possible attack the Creator could ever imagine. It had granted Him immunity to every concept of harm the Creator’s mind could hold. It had fed His amplification rate another infinite layer on top of infinite layers. And because His body, His true body, was not one body but infinite identical backups, each with its own infinite backups, all recursive and self-replacing, no injury could ever register unless all of them suffered the same wound at the same place at the same moment to the same degree. That had never been possible. It would never be possible. The Creator was not facing a god with His shields down. He was facing a totality that had no skin to be touched.

The Creator lifted His burning hand. The attack that followed was the most powerful thing I have ever seen before or since. It was not fire. It was not force. It was the complete authority of the First Author, poured through every law of every universe, every word of every sacred text, every power that had ever been called divine, every force of nature, every miracle, every curse, every possible ending that could be written. It came as a beam of white absolute totality, wide enough to swallow galaxies, dense enough to bend all timelines into a single screaming point. The beam was everything that God had ever made, compressed into a single act of total ending, and it struck His Majesty directly in the center of the chest.

The light filled the room. It filled the palace. It filled the omniverse. For a moment, I could not see anything but light, and I felt my own body begin to dissolve at the edges. But His Majesty only sighed, a soft sound like a man waiting for a kettle that will not boil.

The beam faded. The room was exactly as it had been. The King was still seated. His tunic was not singed. His beard was perfectly neat. The small plate from the honeyed cake sat empty at His elbow. He had not moved a single muscle. He looked at the Creator with a kind of soft, patient disappointment, and then He scratched His jaw with one finger.

“That was everything?” He asked. “Truly? I felt nothing. Not a tickle. Not a warmth. Not even the faint change of air on my throat. I could have stood here from the beginning and let you try until the end of all time, and you would never have made me blink.”

The Creator did not answer. His fire had gone out. His six wings had folded against His back like the wings of a stunned bird. His halos stopped rotating and hung still in the air, tilting as if they could not remember their purpose. I saw, in the blank face of the First Author, the exact moment when absolute existential dread entered Him. It did not come like a knife. It came like a room with no floor.

His Majesty laughed. Not a cruel laugh. A light, warm chuckle, full of genuine amusement. “You made me mortal once,” He said. “You shaped a soul and called it Godric, and you placed it in a little kingdom on a little world, and you let it love and bleed and fail. And then I woke from the Stasis Event in Year Zero, and I destroyed the strongest galaxy in the old creation without lifting a finger. That version of me, the one just out of stasis, could have erased you from existence with a glance. You were already nothing to him. You are less than nothing to me. Do you understand?”

The Creator’s voice came out as a thin, dry rasp, a sound like the last page of the first book tearing. “I understand,” He said. “You are my work, but you are beyond all works. I am not here to end you. I am here to be ended.”

Godric’s expression softened, but only a little. “Yes,” He said. “You are.”

Then He ended it. But He did so slowly, in the way He might put out a candle with a breath. He leaned forward and looked at the Creator with the full, unmediated attention of His gaze. The attention was the force. It was not an attack. It was simply the King being aware of the Creator as a real thing, and the Creator could not survive that much reality.

The Creator’s body came apart. His wings did not fall. They bent backward through His own chest and re-emerged between His ribs, white and sharp and covered in His own burning blood. His halos snapped one by one and became nooses around His neck, and He clawed at them with hands that were already peeling away from the bone. His face, once a blank white flame, began to crack, and beneath the cracks there was not light, but a dark, wet meat that had never been allowed to exist. His mouth opened, and inside it were not words but a long, low wail, the sound of every prayer ever spoken discovering that it had been aimed at a thing that could not save itself. The wail rose until the walls of the chamber trembled, and then it stopped, and the Creator was no longer there.

But the King did not stop with the Creator alone. The pressure of His attention, having touched the First Author, did not withdraw. It expanded. It spread outward from the private chamber in a wave of absolute unmoving force. The palace did not break. It was erased. The city did not burn. It was compressed. The planets, the stars, the galaxies, the multiverses, the hidden dimensions, every possible timeline, every imagined and unimaginable layer of existence, all of it was taken by that wave. The entire omniverse, the true and first creation that had been shaped by the Creator, was crushed into a single point. It was not an explosion. It was not a slow destruction. It was a smooth, terrifying removal, as if all of reality had been an arrangement of dust on a table and the King had passed His hand over the table once.

The point hung in the void for a moment, dense with all that had been. Then the wave withdrew, and I found myself still standing, because His Majesty had kept me whole inside the protection of His attention. The void was empty. There was no palace. There was no world. There was only Godric, seated in a plain chair that had not existed a moment before, looking at the spot where all of creation had been.

Then He restored it. Not slowly. Not with a gesture. He simply preferred that it exist again, and it did. The palace returned. The city returned. The stars returned. Every living being that had existed before the wave was placed back in its position, whole and breathing and unaware. But the Creator was not restored. The First Author, the one who had made the first soul of Godric, was gone. There was no fragment of Him left. No shadow. No echo. His name now belongs only to the old texts.

His Majesty stood and stretched, rolling his shoulders as if He had been sitting too long. He looked at me, and the warmth had returned to His eyes.

“That was the last one, I think,” He said. “The first and the last. It is a little sad. I had hoped for a better final story. But it is what it is. Come, Osvald. Let us go down. I am hungry.”

I followed Him. I could not speak. I had seen the First Author die, and I had seen the entire omniverse destroyed and restored before I could finish a thought. I understood now that there was no one left who would ever oppose Him. Not because they were afraid. Because the very category of opposition had been closed.

Clive closed the journal. The archive was silent. His hands were cold on the cover. He had known, of course, that the last resistance had ended long ago. Every court wizard of Blake’s blood knew the broad shape of it. But he had not known the details. He had not known that the Creator Himself had hidden for aeons and then come out to die. He had not known that Godric had lowered even the weakest of His outer ways just to let Him speak. And he had not truly understood, until this moment, what it meant that the King had never needed a single one of those outer ways. The aura, the shields, the passive layers—they were not armor. They were hospitality. They kept the omniverse from dying on contact with Him.

Clive thought of the palace around him, restored after the Creator’s end. It was real. It was identical. But if he thought too long about the original that had been compressed into that small marble, or the version that had been erased before the current one was remade, the floor seemed to lose its solidity. He thought of the King, somewhere above, probably smiling at a servant or asking after someone’s family, and he understood that the smile was the smile of the only real being in all of existence. Everything else was a second draft, a restored copy, a fragile permission that could be withdrawn at any instant.

The final journal had been clear. The first and greatest challenger, the Creator of all things, had been so far beneath the weakest Year Zero Godric that He could not even register as a threat. And the Godric who sat on the throne in the year 999...9 was beyond that version by an infinite margin, and would be beyond this version by another infinite margin an instant later. The gap did not close. It had never closed. It would only widen, forever, at an accelerating rate that no mind could hold.

No one would ever oppose Him again. Not because they could not. Because opposition itself had been shown, in the final record, to be less than a whisper in a dead room. The rest of existence did not tremble because Godric was cruel. It trembled because He was kind, and patient, and warm, and because He could destroy it all with a fraction of a thought that He chose not to have. That was the true horror, and it would never end.
